card: Paper card. Question: What distinguishes multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs) from traditional solid solutions, and how does local chemical order (LCO) influence dislocation behavior and mechanical strength?. System: FCC NiCoCr medium-entropy alloy (equiatomic composition). Processing: Hybrid molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations with annealing temperatures (Ta) ranging from 650 K to 1650 K; empirical embedded-atom method (EAM) potential developed without spin polarization; simulation box ~52 nm × 6 nm × 52 nm with 1,584,000 atomic sites; 270,000–500,000 MC cycles for convergence.. Test conditions: Energy pathway calculations at 0 K; dislocation motion simulations at 300 K under constant shear stress of 300 MPa; strain rate of 10^-3 s^-1 for CRSS estimation; activation barrier calculations via minimum energy path (MEP).. Findings: Configurational entropy (Sc) rarely reaches the ideal value (Sc,ideal); at 1650 K, Sc is ~95% of Sc,ideal, but drops significantly as LCO develops at lower Ta.; Complex stacking fault energy (CSFE) varies from -24.0 mJ/m² (random solid solution) to ~57 mJ/m² (strong LCO at 650 K).; Local antiphase boundary energies (APBEs) increase from ~50 mJ/m² to ~112 mJ/m² as Ta decreases from 1650 K to 650 K.; Twin boundary energy (γB) in LCO samples increases linearly with the number of transformed layers (λ), unlike elemental FCC metals where it converges.; Dislocations move via intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) rather than smooth propagation, with effective barriers of ~0.15 eV even at 400 MPa shear stress.; Shear stress required to drive dislocation motion increases by a factor of three when the alloy is annealed at 650 K compared to the random state.; Critical resolved shear strength (CRSS) for the random NiCoCr state is ~70 MPa at 300 K and 10^-3 s^-1, consistent with experimental values of ~69 ± 3 MPa.. Mechanism: LCO creates a rugged energy landscape with spatially heterogeneous complex stacking fault energies (CSFE) and antiphase boundary energies (APBE). This heterogeneity acts as nanoscale obstacles that trap dislocation segments, forcing them to move via a nanoscale segment detrapping (NSD) mechanism. The energy required to break LCOs during slip and twinning increases activation barriers and lattice friction, leading to strengthening.. Limitations: The study uses a non-magnetic EAM potential which does not explicitly consider spin polarization; magnetic effects could alter energy differences by ~15 meV/atom. The simulations assume a single-phase solution without second-phase precipitation. Kinetic limitations in experiments may prevent the formation of predicted LCO states at low temperatures within typical homogenization times.. Future work: The authors propose using rapid cooling to obtain a random solid solution for ductility, followed by aging at elevated temperatures to induce LCO for strength. They suggest that the variability in LCO offers a new knob for property tuning in single-phase alloys.. Quote: "The LCO heightens the ruggedness of the energy landscape and raises activation barriers governing dislocation activities."

Paper card. Question: How does local chemical order (LCO) affect local dislocation segment activation barriers in multi-principal element alloys?. System: Multi-principal element alloys (specifically samples with equilibrium LCOs at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K). Processing: Hybrid MD and MC simulations on 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm samples (30 samples per condition) at Ta = 650, 950, and 1350 K; quenched to 0 K; cylinder configurations (20 nm diameter, 10 nm length) cut with a partial dislocation of screw character introduced; quasi-static athermal shearing employed; MEPs calculated using the simplified and improved string method with FIRE algorithm (reparameterization every 10 increments, convergence <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations). Test conditions: Temperatures of 650 K, 950 K, and 1350 K for equilibrium LCO; 0 K for energy minimization; athermal stress limit via quasi-static shearing. Findings: 30 different samples were obtained for each processing condition to ensure meaningful statistics; Sample dimensions were 20 nm × 20 nm × 10 nm along x[11¯0], y[1¯1¯1¯], and z[112¯]; Cylinder configurations had a diameter of 20 nm and axial direction along [112¯]; Dislocation line length was 10 nm as detrapping processes are on the nanoscale; Outer layers of atoms with thickness >2x potential cutoff radius were fixed during energy minimization; Inner cylindrical region with 10 nm diameter was used to calculate average local shear stress; Convergence criterion for MEP calculation was displacement <10–3 Å or 3000 iterations. Mechanism: The authors employed hybrid MD and MC simulations to obtain equilibrium LCOs and then used the string method to calculate minimum energy pathways (MEPs) for dislocation segments, aiming to examine LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers.. Quote: "In order to examine the LCO effects on local dislocation segment activation barriers, hybrid MD and MC simulations were performed"

card: Paper card. Question: How do the strength, ductility, and fracture toughness of an equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy compare to high-entropy alloys and conventional materials, particularly at cryogenic temperatures, and what mechanisms drive these properties?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA). Processing: Arc-melted high-purity elements (>99.9%) under argon, drop-cast into copper moulds, homogenized at 1,200 °C for 24 h, cold-forged and cross-rolled to ~10 mm thickness (60% reduction), then annealed at 800 °C for 1 h in air to achieve a recrystallized microstructure with 5–50 μm grains.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with a strain rate of 10⁻³ s⁻¹; Compact-tension (C(T)) fracture toughness tests at 293 K, 198 K, and 77 K with fatigue pre-cracking and side-grooving per ASTM E1820.. Findings: At 77 K, yield strength reached 657 MPa and ultimate tensile strength reached 1,311 MPa, representing a ~50% increase from room temperature.; Tensile ductility (failure strain) increased to ~0.9 (90%) at 77 K, a ~25% increase from room temperature.; Fracture toughness (KJIc) at crack initiation increased from 208 MPa m1/2 at 293 K to 273 MPa m1/2 at 77 K.; Crack-growth toughness at 77 K reached critical stress-intensity values of ~430 MPa m1/2 (J ~900 kJ m⁻²).; The alloy exhibited a high strain-hardening exponent (n) of 0.4 at cryogenic temperatures.; The CrCoNi alloy showed ~15% higher tensile strength, ~30% higher ductility, and ~50% higher work of fracture than the five-component CrMnFeCoNi alloy at room temperature.; At 77 K, the CrCoNi alloy displayed ~25% higher KJIc, ~27% higher ductility, and ~31% higher work of fracture compared to the CrMnFeCoNi alloy.. Mechanism: The exceptional damage tolerance results from continuous steady strain hardening that suppresses plastic instability, driven by pronounced dislocation activity and deformation-induced nano-twinning. Nano-twinning acts as a dominant deformation mode that provides a steady source of strain hardening, delaying necking and accommodating strain, with its intensity increasing as temperature decreases from room temperature to 77 K.. Limitations: The yield strength at 77 K was slightly lower than the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, attributed to the non-uniform grain size of the current material; the volume fraction of void-initiating inclusions was not accurately quantified relative to the five-component alloy.. Future work: Further studies are needed to accurately determine the relative volume fractions of void-initiating inclusions in the MEA and HEA and to identify their chemistry and crystal structure by TEM after extraction from the voids.. Quote: "strength, ductility and toughness of the CrCoNi alloy improve to strength levels above 1.3 GPa, failure strains up to 90% and KJIc values of 275 MPa m1/2."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the exceptional damage tolerance (high strength, ductility, and fracture toughness) of the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy?. System: CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy (single-phase fcc solid solution). Processing: Arc-melting high-purity elemental starting materials, drop casting into copper moulds, cold forging and cross rolling at room temperature, recrystallization at 800 °C (grain size ∼6 μm), followed by ion milling (5 kV) or twin jet polishing (10 °C, 13 mA/12 V) to create electron-transparent foils with cracks. Test conditions: In situ straining in an aberration-corrected TEM (FEI Tecnai G2 F20, 200 kV) at room temperature using pulsed tensile loading (axial displacement rate ∼1.0 μm s⁻¹). Findings: Early deformation is dominated by the easy motion of Shockley partial dislocations (1/6<112> type) and the continuous nucleation/annihilation of stacking faults (SFs).; Interactions between partials on different {111} planes form stable 'stacking-fault parallelepipeds' (volume defects) that act as formidable obstacles for dislocation motion.; Perfect (undissociated, 1/2<110> type) dislocations move with extreme difficulty in localized bands of planar slip, creating strong barriers that arrest fast-moving partial dislocations.; The motion of perfect dislocations requires overcoming continuous activation barriers, indicative of high friction stress in the alloy.; Nanoscale voids form in the 'semi-cohesive zone' at the intersection of two {111} slip planes, creating fiber-like bridges spanning the crack faces.; These nanobridges (size <200 nm, some ∼100 nm) deform primarily via nano-twinning ({111} twin structure), which accommodates strain and shields the crack tip.; The synergy of these mechanisms yields tensile strength ∼1 GPa, ductility ∼60–70%, and fracture toughness K_JIc > 200 MPa√m.. Mechanism: The authors propose a synergistic sequence where intrinsic toughening arises from easy partial dislocation motion (ductility) followed by strain hardening via stacking-fault parallelepipeds and planar slip bands (strength). Extrinsic toughening occurs via nanoscale twinned bridges that form behind the crack tip, carrying load and shielding the crack tip from the applied driving force.. Limitations: The study notes that 'ultrahigh-resolution observations have to be made at the nanoscale to permit any characterization of mechanisms so close to the crack tip,' and that 'thin foil samples must be used which, under load, cannot display the full constraint of a bulk sample.'. Future work: The authors state that 'further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design of advanced metallic materials with unprecedented damage tolerance.'. Quote: "We identify a synergy of multiple deformation mechanisms, rarely achieved in metallic alloys, which generates high strength, work hardening and ductility"

card: Paper card. Question: How can twinning be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic high-entropy alloys with negative or very small positive stacking fault energies, challenging existing phenomenological models?. System: Fe80−xMnxCo10Cr10 (30 ≤ x ≤ 45), CrMnFeCoNi, and CrCoNi. Test conditions: Temperature range from 100 K to 500 K; affine shear strains of 0.8% and 1.2%; paramagnetic state modeled by disordered local magnetic moment approximation. Findings: For Fe80−xMnxCo10 alloys, twinning is favored over stacking faults when Mn content x ≥ 33, despite the fcc lattice being thermodynamically unstable (negative ΔF).; The metastable twinning (MTW) phenomenon occurs in CrMnFeCoNi between approximately 300 K and 460 K, where twinning is activated despite negative ΔF.; All three studied alloys exhibit γusf ≈ γutf with small or negative intrinsic stacking fault energy (γisf), a shape distinct from conventional fcc alloys.; Increasing affine shear strain increases the difference (γ¯SF - γ¯TW), thereby favoring twin nucleation; for CrMnFeCoNi, strains ≳0.7% induce MTW at all temperatures below ~460 K.; The twinning fraction (fTW) in alloys exhibiting MTW can surpass the previously established upper limit of 50%; for Fe40Mn40Co10Cr10, fTW is calculated to be 53%.; Classical SFE-based models fail to predict twinning in these systems because they require positive SFE > 10–16 mJ m−2, whereas MTW occurs with SFE values between -16.5 and 2.3 mJ m−2.; The condition for MTW is defined by δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where δ is the deviation from the universal scaling law and σ* is the pseudo-interfacial energy (approx. 4–9 mJ m−2).. Mechanism: Twinning is driven by the specific shape of the generalized stacking fault energy (γ-surface) where γusf ≈ γutf and γisf is small or negative, combined with the effect of inherent affine shear strain prior to slip. This strain increases the effective energy barrier for stacking faults relative to twinning, allowing twinning to dominate even when the fcc phase is thermodynamically unstable (ΔF ≤ 0). The phenomenon is governed by the condition δ < γisf/2 < σ*, where the chemistry and strain conditions allow the system to cross deformation mode boundaries that traditional models predict should lead to martensitic transformation.. Limitations: The study notes that while MTW is predicted for CrCoNi with increasing affine shear strain, the specific temperature range for this behavior was not fully explored in the provided text compared to the other alloys, and the analysis relies on theoretical calculations of intrinsic material parameters.. Future work: The authors propose that the disclosed behavior calls for a critical revision of previously adopted design criteria regarding twinning-induced plasticity and suggests opportunities for optimizing the mechanical response in engineering materials by tailoring metastable twinning.. Quote: "We demonstrate that twinning can be the primary deformation mode in metastable face-centered cubic alloys with a fraction that surpasses the previously established upper limit."

card: Paper card. Question: How can supervised learning strategies combining canonical correlation analysis (CCA) and genetic algorithms (GA) be used to efficiently screen the vast compositional space of high-entropy alloys (HEAs) to identify candidates with high hardness and reasonable ductility?. System: Multi-principal element alloys and high-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprising 5 or more elements; specifically, a 16-element palette (Co, Cr, Fe, Ni, Al, Cu, Mn, Ti, Mo, Nb, Ta, V, W, Zr, Zn, Sn) and synthesized candidates including Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03 and Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.. Processing: Synthesis of candidate alloys via arc-melting compressed pellets of elemental, high-purity powders (Sigma-Aldrich, purity ≥99.9%); pellets were remelted four times to ensure homogeneity; resulting as-cast solid pieces were polished for micro-hardness testing.. Test conditions: Vicker's indentation hardness testing using a LECO LM 248AT model hardness tester with a 100 g load applied for 10 s; at least 20 indents conducted per alloy; ductility assessed via optical microscopic inspection of indentations for cracks.. Findings: A multiple regression analysis of 82 HE alloys yielded a correlation coefficient of 0.79 ± 0.07 between alloy metrics and normalized hardness.; Canonical correlation analysis identified three predictor variables especially relevant to hardness: ΔS′mix (positively correlated), ΔH′mix (negatively correlated), and VEC′ (negatively correlated).; A genetic algorithm (GA) with 1000 generations successfully evolved a population of alloys with fitness values 10–15% greater than the maximum found in the original dataset.; Seven candidate alloys synthesized by arc-melting were tested; five of the seven measured hardnesses fell within the 90% prediction interval of the model.; The highest measured hardness was 1084 ± 37 HV for Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03.; The second highest measured hardness was 1011 ± 20 HV for Ti18Ni24Ta12Cr22Co24.; All seven synthesized alloys exhibited Pugh ductility ratios (P) less than 0.5, with some showing moderate to considerable ductility (>50% of indentations without cracks).; Microstructural analysis of the hardest alloy (Co33W07Al33Nb24Cr03) revealed a dendritic structure with 13 vol.% inter-dendritic phase, where the hardness was attributed to significant volume fraction of Nb–W solid solution strengthening.. Mechanism: The authors argue that compositional disorder (high ΔS′mix) enhances hardness, while phase separation (high ΔH′mix) and high valence electron concentration (high VEC′) are associated with lower hardness. The high hardness of specific alloys is attributed to solid solution strengthening from significant volume fractions of Nb–W phases, whereas lower hardness in others may result from non-uniform element distribution or the presence of Ta.. Limitations: The authors note that the Pugh criterion is an empirical proxy for ductility and serves as a rough predictor; they also state that further microstructural and computational analysis is needed to confirm the statistical insights regarding the physics of hardness; additionally, the hardest alloy showed some brittleness with cracking near indentation corners.. Future work: The authors propose using the methodology to investigate the impact of processing on property measurements (e.g., mechanical alloying vs. arc-melting), applying the CCA and GA to other properties like yield strength or corrosion resistance, and performing multi-objective Pareto optimization to simultaneously maximize hardness and ductility.. Quote: "We describe here a supervised learning strategy for the efficient screening of HE alloys that combines two complementary tools, namely: (1) a multiple regression analysis and its generalization, a canonical-correlation analysis (CCA) and (2) a genetic algorithm (GA) with a CCA-inspired fitness function."

card: Paper card. Question: Can an entropy-forming-ability (EFA) descriptor based on first-principles energy distribution spectra predict the synthesizability of disordered five-metal refractory carbides as homogeneous high-entropy single phases?. System: Five-metal refractory carbides (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5, HfMoTaWZrC5, HfMoTiWZrC5, HfMoVWZrC5) derived from eight metals (Hf, Nb, Mo, Ta, Ti, V, W, Zr) and carbon. Processing: Solid-state synthesis via ball milling (2 h total, 30-min intervals with 10-min rests) followed by Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS) at 2200 °C, 100 °C/min heating rate, 30 MPa uniaxial pressure, 5-min dwell in vacuum/argon atmosphere. Test conditions: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification; Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) for chemical homogeneity; Nanoindentation at 27 °C ± 0.5 °C with 50 mN load for Vickers hardness (HV) and elastic modulus (E); Williamson–Hall analysis for lattice strain. Findings: The EFA descriptor correctly predicted that MoNbTaVWC5 (EFA = 125 (eV/atom)−1), HfNbTaTiZrC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1), and HfNbTaTiVC5 (EFA = 100 (eV/atom)−1) would form homogeneous single phases, while HfMoVWZrC5 (EFA = 37 (eV/atom)−1) would not.; Six of the nine synthesized compositions (MoNbTaVWC5, HfNbTaTiZrC5, HfNbTaTiVC5, HfNbTaTiWC5, NbTaTiVWC5, HfTaTiWZrC5) exhibited single rock-salt fcc phases, whereas the three lowest-EFA compositions showed multiple secondary phases.; Vickers hardness of HfNbTaTiZrC5 reached 32 GPa, which is 50% higher than the rule of mixtures (ROM) prediction, and HfTaTiWZrC5 reached 33 GPa.; The Pearson correlation between the inverse EFA (EFA−1) and lattice distortion (ε) was 0.97, and the Spearman rank correlation was 0.98, validating EFA as a synthesizability descriptor.; Lattice distortion (ε) ranged from 0.063% for MoNbTaVWC5 (most homogeneous) to 0.325% for HfMoVWZrC5 (least homogeneous).; The highest-EFA composition MoNbTaVWC5 formed a homogeneous phase despite using precursors Mo2C and W2C with different structures (orthorhombic and hexagonal) and stoichiometries compared to the rock-salt product.; Vibrational contributions to formation free energy at 2000 K ranged from ~0 meV/atom to −31 meV/atom, which are significantly smaller than the configurational entropy contributions required to overcome formation enthalpy barriers (50–150 meV/atom).; A threshold of EFA ~50 (eV/atom)−1 was identified as the point above which homogeneous disordered single phases are likely to form.. Mechanism: The authors argue that a narrow energy distribution spectrum (low standard deviation σ) implies a low energy cost to access metastable configurations, promoting configurational randomness (entropy) at finite temperatures. This entropy stabilization allows the disordered rock-salt phase to remain locked in upon cooling, even when competing ordered phases exist. Enhanced hardness is attributed to mass disorder causing impedance mismatch that scatters dislocations, increasing resistance to plastic deformation.. Limitations: The study notes that the Williamson–Hall formalism does not provide particularly accurate absolute values of lattice strain (ε), though it is effective for relative comparisons. Additionally, the vibrational contribution to entropy is an order of magnitude smaller than configurational entropy, and the study did not investigate the specific effect of carbon stoichiometry on melting points.. Future work: The authors state that an investigation of the effect of carbon stoichiometry is clearly warranted to understand how vacancies might further improve high-temperature performance, although it is outside the scope of this study.. Quote: "The descriptor correctly predicts the ease with which compositions can be experimentally synthesized as rock-salt high-entropy homogeneous phases, validating the ansatz, and in some cases, going beyond intuition."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the number of principal elements (N) in equimolar multi-principal element alloys affect the probability of forming disordered solid solution (SS) phases versus intermetallic (IM) phases, and what are the implications for high-temperature structural applications?. System: Equimolar combinations of 3 to 6 elements from a palette of 26 metallic elements (including Al, Si, Mo, Ta, W, Nb, Ti, V, Re, Zr, Cr, Fe, Co, Ni, etc.). Processing: High-throughput computational screening using the CALPHAD method (Pandat v.8.1 software) to calculate phase diagrams for 134,547 equimolar alloy systems; results filtered for credibility where the fraction of fully assessed binary systems (fAB) equals 1.. Test conditions: Phase diagrams calculated between 600 °C and 3,600 °C; properties evaluated at the solidus temperature (Tm) and at 600 °C; maximum use temperature (Tuse) estimated as the lowest of 0.8Tm or the last first-order phase reaction temperature below Tm.. Findings: The fraction of solid solution (SS) alloys decreases as the number of elements (N) increases: at Tm, 30% of 3-component alloys are SS, dropping to only 5% for 6-component alloys.; Configurational entropy rises slowly with N (as ln(N)), while the number of binary interactions increases rapidly (as (N/2)(N−1)), explaining why IM formation becomes more probable as N increases.; The maximum solidus temperature (Tm) decreases with N: 2,925 °C for 3-component, 2,754 °C for 4-component, 2,435 °C for 5-component, and 2,056 °C for 6-component alloys.; The maximum maximum use temperature (Tuse) decreases with N: 2,285 °C for 3-component, 1,846 °C for 4-component, 1,677 °C for 5-component, and 1,159 °C for 6-component alloys.; Only 3 out of 209 SS alloys with Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C are 6-component alloys, whereas 108 are 3-component alloys.; Extreme property values (highest/lowest density, modulus, cost) are achieved in ternary (3-component) alloys, while 6-component alloys show tighter property spreads.; 51 equimolar alloy systems with 3 ≤ N ≤ 5 were identified that satisfy aggressive design criteria (Tuse ≥ 1,000 °C, density ≤ 10 g cm−3, modulus ≥ 100 GPa, cost ≤ $200/kg, no IM phases at Tm).. Mechanism: The authors argue that while configurational entropy (Smix) favors solid solution stability, it increases only logarithmically with the number of elements. Conversely, the number of binary element pairs increases quadratically, raising the probability that at least one pair has a sufficiently large negative formation enthalpy (Hf) to overcome the entropy term in the Gibbs free energy equation (G = H - TS), thereby stabilizing intermetallic phases.. Limitations: The study is restricted to equimolar compositions; non-equimolar alloys were not explored and may offer higher Tm or Tuse values. Additionally, the credibility filter (fAB=1) excluded over 95% of the calculated systems, potentially missing viable alloys if less stringent criteria were acceptable.. Future work: The authors propose extending the screening to non-equimolar alloys to uncover local compositions with extreme properties, conducting more extensive experimental validations to potentially relax credibility criteria, and developing high-throughput experimental techniques capable of handling microstructural length scales.. Quote: "We find the surprising result that solid solution alloys become less likely as the number of alloy elements increases."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the heterogeneous lattice strain field, caused by severe atomic lattice distortion in multi-principal element alloys (MPEAs), influence 3D dynamic dislocation evolution, strengthening mechanisms, and the strength-ductility synergy?. System: FeCoCrNiMn multi-principal element alloy (Cantor alloy). Processing: Arc-melting in high-purity argon atmosphere with raw materials ≥99.9 wt.% purity; remelted at least four times; cast into 10 mm diameter cylindrical ingots; heat treated at 1,200 °C for 30 h; micropillars milled via FIB with ~2 μm diameter, aspect ratio ~2, and taper angles <2.5°. Test conditions: Micropillar compression tests conducted at room temperature using a Hysitron TI 950 TriboIndenter; DDD simulations performed with ParaDiS code on a 5.5 μm cube with periodic boundary conditions at a strain rate of 10^4/s; lattice strain measured via Geometric Phase Analysis (GPA) on TEM images. Findings: Root-mean-square lattice strain shows a power law decaying relation with scan size, consistent with a fractal distribution of the residual strain field.; Heterogeneous lattice strain causes dislocation motion to become 'sluggish' with multiple pinning sites, raising dislocation density and entanglement probability.; Dislocations exhibit multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips (double cross slip) to minimize local lattice resistance.; The presence of heterogeneous lattice strain leads to a significant increase in yield strength compared to simulations without it.; Dislocation double cross slip results in the formation of dislocation walls and a unique multijogged dislocation configuration.; Yielding strengths predicted by DDD simulations for different crystallographic orientations are consistent with experimental micropillar measurements.; The root-mean-square lattice strain, extrapolated from high-resolution TEM images, correlates positively with the yield strengths of the MPEAs.. Mechanism: The heterogeneous lattice strain field creates a fluctuating elastic stress field that acts as pinning sites for dislocations. This forces dislocations to adopt wavy trajectories involving 'pinning-and-depinning' processes, which hinders smooth movement and promotes the formation of multiple kinks/jogs and bidirectional cross slips. These behaviors increase dislocation density, entanglement, and forest strengthening, thereby enhancing strain hardening and enabling the strength-ductility synergy.. Limitations: The study does not account for the coupling of chemical short-range order (SRO) with lattice distortion, noting that while SRO may increase local shear strains, this is beyond the scope of the current work.. Future work: To address the effect of chemical short-range order (SRO) on local lattice strain and its coupling with lattice distortion in altering mechanical properties.. Quote: "Our experiments and simulations clearly show that the heterogeneous strain field can contribute to the enhanced mechanical properties of multi–principal element alloys through the new heterogeneous strain-induced strengthening mechanisms"

card: Paper card. Question: What alloying and scaling conditions lead to the strongest both ductile and stable materials?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (HEA) thin films and pillars. Processing: d.c. magnetron co-sputtering on (100) silicon or sapphire substrates at room temperature; Ion beam-assisted deposition (IBAD) used with 1.2 keV beam energy, 5 mA current, and 35° incidence angle to reduce grain size; Focused Ga ion beams (FIB) used to mill pillars with diameters of ~1 μm, 500, 200, and 100 nm. Test conditions: Microcompression tests at a strain rate of 2 × 10−3 s−1; Thermal annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days in argon atmosphere. Findings: HEA pillars exhibit extraordinarily high yield strengths of ~10 GPa, one order of magnitude higher than the bulk form.; Compressive plastic strains over 30% were achieved in smaller pillars without cracking.; 580-nm Normal HEA pillars show a yield strength of ~5 GPa, while 580-nm IBAD HEA pillars reach ~6.5 GPa.; Smallest IBAD HEA pillars (~70–100 nm diameter) exhibit yield strengths of ~8–10 GPa.; After annealing at 1,100 °C for 3 days, HEA pillars retain a high yield strength of ~5 GPa, whereas pure W films show significant grain growth and pore formation.; IBAD HEA pillars exhibit a log–log slope of −0.2 for the relationship between flow stress and pillar diameter, indicating the lowest size dependence among reported pillars.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh strength is attributed to the simultaneous operation of four strengthening mechanisms: lattice friction, Taylor hardening, source-controlled strength, and grain-boundary strengthening. The excellent thermal stability is attributed to relatively low grain-boundary energy due to the highly disordered grain interiors in HEAs, which lowers the driving force for grain-boundary migration compared to pure metals.. Limitations: The text notes that large pillars (>1 μm) experience cracking at strains larger than ~20% and that the smallest pillars (~70–100 nm) show higher scattering levels in strength due to inhomogeneous distribution of grain boundaries.. Future work: The authors state that mechanical tests for small-scale HEAs at high temperatures are still needed to prove their capability as high-temperature materials, and that further work is required to optimize small-scale HEAs for applications, such as determining the best alloying elements and optimized grain and specimen size combinations.. Quote: "Here we report a strategy for the fabrication of refractory HEA thin films and small-sized pillars that consist of strongly textured, columnar and nanometre-sized grains."

Processing: Arc-melting of high-purity elements in argon, cold-rolling (60% reduction), recrystallization at 1,173–1,473 K; single-crystal micropillars (1.0–8.3 μm edge length) machined via FIB at 30 kV; bulk polycrystals with grain sizes of 8, 70, and 340 μm. Test conditions: Micropillar compression at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10⁻¹ s⁻¹); bulk polycrystal compression at room temperature and 77 K (strain rate 1 × 10⁻⁴ s⁻¹); TEM analysis at 200 kV. Findings: Bulk room temperature CRSS is estimated at 33–43 MPa, approximately 10 times higher than that of pure nickel (~3.2 MPa).; CRSS follows an inverse power-law scaling with pillar size with an exponent of –0.63, independent of crystal orientation.; Stacking fault energy is determined to be 30 ± 5 mJ/m² based on Shockley partial separations of 3.5–4.5 nm (screw) and 5–8 nm (edge).; Yield stress at 77 K (260 MPa for 340 μm grain size) is slightly more than twice the yield stress at room temperature (127 MPa).; Dislocations are planar and smoothly curved with no preferred line orientation, indicating no significant anisotropy in edge and screw mobilities.; The shear-modulus-normalized CRSS of the HEA corresponds to a hypothetical binary alloy with 20–50 at.% solute concentration and ~4% atomic size misfit.; Young's and shear moduli are ~10% smaller than pure Ni, while the bulk modulus is 24% smaller than pure Ni.. Mechanism: The high CRSS is attributed to thermal solid-solution hardening driven by atomic size misfit (~4% between Cr and Co/Fe) rather than severe lattice distortion alone; the low stacking fault energy combined with a high shear modulus leads to wide partial separations that inhibit cross-slip, while the absence of orientation dependence suggests similar mobilities for edge and screw segments.. Limitations: The study notes that Goldschmidt radii may not provide accurate size misfit values, requiring ab initio calculations to estimate the true misfit of ~4.1%; the solid-solution hardening estimate is described as a rough order-of-magnitude calculation.. Future work: The authors state that full results of deformation experiments on bulk single crystals of the HEA will be published elsewhere and that additional studies are needed to improve understanding of factors like impurity contamination affecting CRSS.. Quote: "CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation."

card: Paper card. Question: How local chemistry affects enhanced deformation mechanisms and the origin of strain hardening in dual-phase high-entropy alloys.. System: Cantor-like Cr20Mn6Fe34Co34Ni6 high-entropy alloy (at.%) comprising face-centered cubic (fcc) austenite and hexagonal closed packed (hcp) ε-martensite phases.. Processing: Vacuum induction casting of 4-kg ingots, hot rolling at 900 °C (50% reduction), homogenization at 1200 °C for 3 h with water quenching, cold rolling to 40–50% thickness reduction, and recrystallization annealing at 800 °C for 1 h followed by water quenching.. Test conditions: Uniaxial tensile testing at room temperature (strain rate 1 × 10−3 s−1); in situ TEM straining at ambient temperature (200 kV, loading rate ~1 μm/s); nanoscale pillar compression (300 nm diameter, 2 nm/s displacement rate).. Findings: The alloy exhibits a tensile strength approaching 1 GPa and ductility of almost 60% at ambient temperatures.; Partial dislocation activities result in stable three-dimensional stacking-fault networks comprising multiple stacking faults and sessile Lomer–Cottrell locks.; The fraction of the stronger hcp phase progressively increases during plastic deformation by forming at the stacking-fault network boundaries in the fcc phase.; Dual-phase pillars displayed the highest ultimate strength at ~3.45 GPa, compared to ~2.25 GPa for pure hcp and ~1.25 GPa for pure fcc pillars.; Local chemical composition variations show Ni atomic fraction fluctuating from −58% to 115% about its average, with Mn near stacking faults being nearly 30% higher than in the matrix.; The continuous fcc → hcp phase transformation sustains a hardening effect where flow stress increases two-fold from 1.75 to ~3.5 GPa.; Lomer–Cottrell locks act to immobilize dislocation motion and provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation.. Mechanism: The authors argue that variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of stable 3D stacking-fault networks. These networks impede dislocation motion (work hardening) and serve as preferred sites for the nucleation and growth of the hcp phase via a transformation-induced plasticity (TRIP) effect, where the continuous increase in the hcp volume fraction drives the ultrahigh strain hardening.. Limitations: The fracture toughness of these TRIP HEAs may not be similarly enhanced compared to the Cantor alloy, particularly at decreasing temperatures, because the product hcp ε-martensite phase tends to be quite brittle.. Future work: The authors propose that the intentional generation of Lomer–Cottrell locks raises a fundamental question of how to increase the probability of interactions between dissociated dislocations with the sole objective of enhancing the formation of such locks.. Quote: "variations in local chemical composition promote a high density of Lomer-Cottrell locks, which facilitate the construction of the stacking-fault networks to provide nucleation sites for the hcp phase transformation."

card: Paper card. Question: Can the thermodynamic principle of high entropy stabilization be applied to design self-regenerative supported transition metal catalysts that resist sintering through reversible exsolution-dissolution cycles?. System: Cubic high-entropy oxide Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox (Zr:Ni:Fe:Cu:Mn:Co molar ratio 5:1:1:1:1:1) and comparative binary/ternary doped ZrO2 systems (e.g., Zr0.5Cu0.5Ox, Zr0.5(CuMn)0.5Ox). Processing: Mechanochemical synthesis: ZrCl4, NiCl2, FeCl3, CuCl2·2H2O, MnCl2, CoCl2·6H2O, and NaCl were ball-milled for 2 hours total; NaOH was added and milled for 1 hour; calcination in air at 550 °C for 3 hours (heating rate 2 K min−1); followed by washing with water and ethanol and drying at 70 °C. Test conditions: Redox cycling: H2 treatment at 600 °C for 2 h followed by Air treatment at 550 °C; Catalytic testing: CO2 hydrogenation (RWGS) at 400 °C for >500 h continuous operation; Feed gas H2:CO2 = 3:1 at atmospheric pressure. Findings: The high entropy Zr0.5(NiFeCuMnCo)0.5Ox achieved a specific surface area of 84 m2 g−1 due to mild crystallization at 550 °C and mechanochemical particle breakage.; In situ reversible exsolution of CoFeCuNi alloy nanoparticles and reintegration into the ZrO2 matrix were observed over three redox cycles (H2 600 °C + Air 550 °C).; The configurational entropy contribution (TΔSconfig = T × 12.7 J mol−1 K−1) was predominant in the Gibbs free energy (ΔG), driving the stability of the host structure.; During CO2 hydrogenation at 400 °C, the catalyst maintained ~29% CO2 conversion and >90% CO selectivity for over 500 hours without sintering.; Binary doped Zr0.5Cu0.5Ox showed excessive particle growth (average size 37.7 nm) and severe deactivation within 40 hours, unlike the high entropy variant.; Impregnated 5% and 10% NiFeCuCo/ZrOx catalysts suffered severe deactivation within 1–3 hours, whereas the high entropy oxide lasted >500 hours.; XPS analysis confirmed the formation of metallic Co0, Ni0, Cu0, and Fe0 species during H2 reduction, while Mn remained largely as MnO.. Mechanism: The high configurational entropy lowers the Gibbs free energy of the solid solution, stabilizing the host matrix against sintering. During reduction, transition metals exsolve to form active alloy nanoparticles; during oxidation, the entropy-added motivation drives the reintegration of these metals back into the parent oxide lattice, creating a self-regenerative cycle that confines metal species and prevents agglomeration.. Limitations: The study notes that binary and ternary doped ZrO2 samples formed impure phases or showed excessive particle growth, indicating that the high entropy effect is critical for the observed stability; the authors also mention that the exsolved CoFeCuNi NPs could not be described as high entropy alloys themselves.. Future work: The authors propose that the current theory may inspire the design of more supported transition metal catalysts (STMCs) with excellent sintering-resistance performance and suggest that considering entropic contributions is just the beginning for developing unique materials for heterogeneous catalysis.. Quote: "entropy driving force could promote the self-regeneration process is proposed"

card: Paper card. Question: Can high-entropy solid solutions be formed in non-oxide ceramic metal diborides with a hexagonal layered structure, and do they exhibit superior hardness and oxidation resistance compared to their constituent individual diborides?. System: Seven equimolar five-component metal diborides: (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Mo0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Mo0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Mo0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Nb0.2Ti0.2)B2, (Hf0.2Zr0.2Ta0.2Cr0.2Ti0.2)B2, and (Hf0.2Zr0.2W0.2Mo0.2Ti0.2)B2. Processing: High-energy ball milling (HEBM) for 6 hours in WC media with 60-minute milling/5-minute cooling cycles, followed by spark plasma sintering (SPS) at 2000 °C for 5 minutes under 30 MPa pressure in vacuum (10^-2 Torr). Test conditions: Hardness measured via Vickers indentation at 200 kgf/mm2 with 15s hold time; oxidation resistance assessed via sequential isothermal annealing in flowing dry air at 800–1500 °C for 1 hour per step. Findings: Six of the seven compositions formed a single-phase hexagonal AlB2 structure with greater than 92% of theoretical density.; Aberration-corrected STEM confirmed 2-D high-entropy metal layers separated by rigid boron nets with no detectable layered segregation along the c-axis.; The measured standard deviations of lattice spacings between basal (0001) planes were only ~0.6% of the average c lattice parameter.; Hardness of the high-entropy diborides was generally greater than the average hardness of the five individual constituent metal diborides.; Oxidation resistance was generally better than the average of individual components, with HEB#1 and HEB#7 maintaining shape at 1500 °C while TiB2 pulverized.; Revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factors based on lattice constants (δc) of 3.9% to 5.2% rationalized single-phase formation, whereas the non-single-phase specimen had δc ≈ 6.2%.; Minor secondary oxide phases ((Zr, Hf)O2) were observed in six specimens, and a secondary (Ti1.6W2.4)B4 phase was found in the W-containing specimen.. Mechanism: The formation of high-entropy solid solutions is rationalized by a revised Hume-Rothery size-difference factor calculated from lattice constants rather than atomic radii; the rigid 2-D boron net constrains the metal layers, reducing the effective size mismatch (δa) and allowing entropy stabilization of the disordered solid solution despite larger atomic size differences in the c-direction.. Limitations: The presence of porosity and oxide inclusions resulting from the HEBM procedure adversely affected hardness and oxidation resistance; MoB2 is metastable at room temperature and W2B5 starting powder has limited solubility; the study did not fully optimize microstructure for maximum property performance.. Future work: Further systematic investigation of hardness, oxidation resistance, and other properties is needed, particularly focusing on processing optimization to achieve fully-dense and oxide-free specimens and utilizing the large compositional design space to tailor protective oxide scales.. Quote: "Greater than 92% of the theoretical densities have been generally achieved with largely uniform compositions from nanoscale to microscale."

System: Mesoporous Mn0.5Ce0.5Ox solid solution (Mn/Ce atomic ratio 1:1). Processing: Slow hydrolysis of Mn(II) acetate and Ce(IV) methoxyethoxide precursors in the presence of ionic liquid BmimTf2N template at 50 °C for 24 h, followed by solidification at 200 °C for 2 h, extraction of the ionic liquid via ethanol reflux, and thermal treatment at 500 °C for 2 h in air.. Test conditions: Cyclohexane oxidation: 100 °C, 1 MPa O2, 12 h reaction time; CO oxidation: 1% CO in dry air, atmospheric pressure, flow rate 10 ml min−1; Other hydrocarbons: 110–120 °C, 1 MPa O2.. Findings: Cyclohexane conversion reached 17.7% with 81% selectivity for KA oil (cyclohexanone/cyclohexanol) at 100 °C.; The catalyst achieved 100% CO conversion at approximately 90 °C, with a T50 of 60 °C.; XPS analysis revealed that Mn4+ species dominate the surface with 87% content.; The atomic ratio of 'reactive' oxygen species (Oβ) on the surface reached 44.1%.; The catalyst maintained activity for at least 20 runs in cyclohexane oxidation without significant loss.; The average crystalline size of the Mn0.5Ce0.5Ox@500 sample was calculated to be 1.4 nm.; The H2 consumption of the Mn0.5Ce0.5Ox@500 sample reached 4.22 mmol g−1.; Oxidation of cyclohexane could proceed at a temperature as low as 80 °C.. Mechanism: The high activity is attributed to the formation of a Mn0.5Ce0.5Ox solid solution with an ultrahigh manganese doping concentration in the CeO2 cubic fluorite lattice, which leads to maximum active surface oxygens for C–H bond activation and highly reducible Mn4+ ions that facilitate the rapid migration of oxygen vacancies from the bulk to the surface.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The authors propose that the self-assembly strategy with ionic liquids will inspire more designs of mesoporous oxide solid solutions for specific tasks in the near future.. card: Paper card. Question: How does entropy stabilization in transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) influence reversible lithium storage capacity, cycling stability, and the underlying reaction mechanism compared to medium entropy oxides?. System: Transition-metal-based high entropy oxides (TM-HEO) with composition (Co0.2Cu0.2Mg0.2Ni0.2Zn0.2)O; compared to 4-cation medium entropy oxides (MEO) such as (Co0.25Cu0.25Zn0.25Ni0.25)O and (Co0.25Cu0.25Mg0.25Zn0.25)O. Processing: Nebulized Spray Pyrolysis (NSP) at 1150 °C; 4-cation systems required post-annealing at 1000 °C for 1 h under ambient atmosphere; electrodes cast with 63 wt% active material, 22 wt% Super C65, 15 wt% PVA binder. Test conditions: Galvanostatic cycling in Li-metal coin cells, voltage range 0.01–3 V vs. Li+/Li, specific currents from 50 to 3000 mA g−1, room temperature, 1 M LiPF6 in EC/DMC or EC/EMC electrolyte. Findings: The 5-cation TM-HEO cycled over 300 cycles at 200 mA g−1 with specific capacities stabilizing around 650 mAh g−1 after initial activation.; The 5-cation system achieved a specific capacity of 770 mAh g−1 after 100 cycles following a rate increase to 3 A g−1 for 5 cycles.; Medium entropy oxides (4-cation systems) showed rapid capacity degradation, with the Co-removed variant failing completely after ~10 cycles.; The Coulombic efficiency of the 5-cation TM-HEO stabilized between 99.4% and 99.95% in the range of cycles 60–400.; The 4-cation system without Zn (TM-MEO(-Zn)) exhibited a two-step oxidation process at 1.7 V and 2.2 V, unlike the single-step oxidation of the 5-cation system.; High-loading electrodes (2.3 mg cm−2) maintained Coulombic efficiencies >98.5% and an areal capacity of 1.3 mAh cm−2 after 30 cycles.; No metallic phases or Cu dendrites were detected via TEM/EDX after 100 cycles, despite the conversion reaction mechanism.. Mechanism: The authors propose that the rock-salt structure is preserved as a permanent host matrix during the entire conversion process. While some cations (e.g., Co, Cu) are reduced to metallic states during lithiation, they remain 'trapped' within the defect-rich rock-salt lattice stabilized by unreduced cations (e.g., Mg, Ni). This entropy stabilization lowers the Gibbs free energy, favoring the re-incorporation of reduced cations into the original lattice sites upon delithiation, preventing phase separation and structural collapse.. Limitations: The theoretical capacity cannot be predicted with high accuracy due to unknown additional processes like Zn-Li alloying or intermetallic formation; some 4-cation systems (TM-MEO(-Mg) and TM-MEO(-Ni)) could not be synthesized as single-phase compounds even at high temperatures.. Future work: Further investigations should be pursued to explore the full potential of high entropy oxide electrode materials, including the addition of other cations (Fe, Mn, Cr, V) to develop a modular method for tailoring electrodes to specific needs.. Quote: "The stabilization effect of entropy brings significant benefits for the storage capacity retention of high entropy oxides and greatly improves the cycling stability."

card: Paper card. Question: Is it feasible to produce the refractory metal high entropy alloy W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 via in-situ alloy formation using laser powder bed fusion (PBF-LB/M) from elemental powders, and how do process parameters influence defect formation, microstructure, and phase composition?. System: W20Mo20Ta20Nb20V20 (refractory metal high entropy alloy) fabricated from a heterogeneous mixture of elemental W, Mo, Ta, Nb, and V powders.. Processing: Laser Powder Bed Fusion (PBF-LB/M) using an AconityMINI machine with a 1 kW fiber laser (1080 nm) on a Mo substrate in Argon atmosphere (<25 ppm O2). Two parameter sets were used: Set A (600 W, 800 mm/s, 120 µm hatch, 125 J/mm³) and Set B (100 W, 100 mm/s, 45 µm hatch, 889 J/mm³). Vanadium powder content was increased by a factor of 1.5 to compensate for evaporation.. Test conditions: Samples (6 × 6 × 6 mm³) were analyzed via optical microscopy, SEM, EBSD, TEM, and microhardness testing. Microhardness was measured as HV0.1. Cooling rates are estimated at 10⁶ K/s.. Findings: Relative densities reached 99.8% for parameter set A and 99.5% for parameter set B.; A single bcc-phase was confirmed by EBSD and TEM, consistent with vacuum arc melted samples.; Average grain size was 16.3 µm for PBF-LB/M B, which is more than four times smaller than the 80 µm reported for vacuum arc melted samples.; Parameter set B (higher volumetric energy density) resulted in fewer undissolved tungsten particles compared to set A.; Parameter set A exhibited smaller cracks than set B, which showed wider cracks due to higher internal stress.; Microhardness of the coarser structure (Set A) was 561 ± 17 HV0.1, while the finer cellular structure (Set B) was 614 ± 21 HV0.1.; Elemental segregation was observed: V concentrated in interdendritic areas, while W and Ta were predominantly in intradendritic areas.; Solidification mode shifted from dendritic (Set A) to cellular (Set B) based on growth rate (R) and temperature gradient (G) conditions.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the formation of undissolved W particles to the high melting point of tungsten, which requires high volumetric energy input and slow scan speeds to dissolve. Cracking is caused by internal stresses from the PBF-LB/M process combined with the alloy's low room temperature ductility and brittle grain boundaries (likely due to O and N impurities). The microstructure (dendritic vs. cellular) is controlled by the ratio of growth rate (R) to temperature gradient (G), where higher R and lower G favor dendrites, while lower R and higher G favor cellular structures.. Limitations: Samples contained cracks and undissolved tungsten particles; completely defect-free samples were not produced. The study notes that the alloy has limited room temperature ductility and fracture toughness.. Future work: The authors suggest using a high-temperature (>600 °C) build-platform heating device and/or high-purity powder with low O and N content to achieve crack-free processing. They also propose verifying if more recently developed refractory metal high entropy alloys with increased room temperature ductility can be processed without high-temperature heating.. Quote: "The relative density of the samples with a dimension of 6 × 6 × 6 mm3 reaches, in dependence of the PBF-LB/M parameter set, 99.8%."

card: Paper card. Question: How can the room temperature ductility of an initially brittle refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) with a continuous ordered B2 matrix be improved while maintaining high yield strength?. System: Al0.5NbTa0.8Ti1.5V0.2Zr (Refractory High Entropy Alloy). Processing: 1. Vacuum/argon arc melting followed by hot isostatic pressing (HIP) at 1200 °C for 2 hours under 210 MPa argon. 2. Homogenization at 1200 °C for 24 hours followed by slow cooling (10 °C/min) to room temperature (Condition 1). 3. Solutionizing Condition 1 at 1400 °C for 20 min followed by water quenching (Condition 2). 4. Annealing Condition 2 at 600 °C for 120 hrs followed by water quenching (Condition 3).. Test conditions: Room temperature (RT) and 600 °C uniaxial compression testing at a strain rate of 0.001 s−1; Vickers microhardness (4.9 N load, 15 s dwell); Microstructural characterization via SEM, TEM, and Atom Probe Tomography (APT).. Findings: Condition (1) (continuous B2 matrix) exhibited a yield strength of 2035 MPa but only 4.5% compressive strain before fracture.; Condition (2) (single-phase weakly ordered BCC) showed high ductility with no fracture after 60% true strain but lower yield strength (1065 MPa).; Condition (3) (inverted microstructure with discrete B2 precipitates in continuous BCC matrix) achieved a yield strength of 1345 MPa and 16.9% peak strain with fracture at 38% strain.; At 600 °C, Condition (3) showed anomalous strengthening with a yield strength of 1423 MPa (higher than its RT value of 1345 MPa) and 16.2% plasticity.; APT analysis revealed strong elemental partitioning: B2 phase is rich in Al and Zr, while BCC phase is rich in Nb and Ta.; The microstructure of Condition (3) consists of discrete B2 precipitates (~50 nm) within a continuous disordered BCC matrix, contrasting with Condition (1) where B2 is the continuous matrix.; Condition (1) hardness was 562 ± 16 HV, Condition (2) was 405 ± 11 HV, and Condition (3) was 475 ± 12 HV.. Mechanism: The authors argue that the poor ductility in Condition (1) is caused by the continuous ordered B2 matrix, which is inherently brittle. The improved ductility in Condition (3) is attributed to the 'inversion' of the microstructure, where the continuous phase becomes the more ductile disordered BCC matrix, while the hard B2 phase exists as discrete precipitates providing strengthening. The anomalous strengthening at 600 °C in Condition (3) is speculated to result from competing slip systems in the complex B2 phase (e.g., <001>{110} and <111>{112}) leading to sessile kinks or dislocation debris, similar to mechanisms in Ni3Al.. Limitations: The authors state that the details of the strengthening mechanisms are beyond the scope of the study and that the explanation for the anomalous strengthening at 600 °C is highly speculative. They note that applying classical precipitation hardening models requires parameters (lattice misfit, elastic properties, fault energies) that are difficult to quantify in this complex RHEA.. Future work: The authors recommend additional scientific studies to establish the influence of concentrated alloy additions on precipitation strengthening parameters, further investigation of deformation mechanisms at room temperature and 600 °C, and additional studies at higher temperatures and under tensile loading.. card: Paper card. Question: Can a single BCC solid solution of NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy be successfully fabricated via selective laser melting (SLM) despite the high melting points of its constituent elements, and what are the resulting microstructural, mechanical, and corrosion properties compared to traditional superalloys?. System: NbMoTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (nominal equiatomic composition: Nb 99.9%, Mo 99.9%, Ta 99.9%, W 99.9%). Processing: Selective Laser Melting (SLM) using FORWEDO LM120 equipment with a 500 W fiber laser in an argon atmosphere (<20 ppm oxygen); initial parameters: hatch distance 0.1 mm, layer thickness 0.1 mm, laser power factor 0.8, scanning velocity 250 mm/s, S-cross scanning; followed by a remelting process (3 total passes per layer) to achieve a linear energy density of up to 2.83 J/mm. Test conditions: Microstructure and composition analyzed via SEM (HITACHI SU-8010) and EDS; crystal structure via XRD (Cu target, λ = 1.54 Å); microhardness measured on XY plane; corrosion resistance tested via potentiodynamic polarization in 3.5 wt% NaCl solution (scanning voltage −0.2 V to +0.2 V) and high-voltage scanning (−1.5 to +2 V). Findings: A single BCC solid solution was formed without secondary phases, with an experimental lattice parameter of 3.2034 Å.; Elements with lower melting points and densities (Nb and Mo) showed negative molar ratio deviations of up to 3.5% (Nb: −3.5 at%, Mo: −0.16 at%) compared to the nominal 25%.; The average grain size was 13.4 μm, significantly smaller than the 200 μm observed in as-cast NbMoTaW HEA.; Primary and secondary dendrite arm spacings were 6.59 μm and 1.68 μm, respectively, much finer than the 20–30 μm spacing in as-cast samples.; The average microhardness of the SLM-fabricated sample reached 826 Hv, compared to 446 Hv for arc-melted HEA and 310–437 Hv for superalloys.; The free-corrosion current (Icorr) of the NbMoTaW HEA was 8.716 × 10−11 A, which is two orders of magnitude lower than that of 316 L steel (8.815 × 10−9 A).; Visual corrosion testing showed 316 L steel suffered up to 1 mm corrosion depth, while the NbMoTaW alloy exhibited only crack extension and minor pitting.. Mechanism: The rapid solidification in SLM creates extremely high temperature gradients and cooling rates, limiting growth time and resulting in fine grains and slender dendrites. Composition deviations occur because powders with lower melting points and densities fuse first, spread over larger areas, absorb more energy, and evaporate earlier during the process. The improved hardness is attributed to grain refinement following the Hall–Petch law, while superior corrosion resistance is due to the presence of easily passivating elements (Nb, Mo, Ta) despite minor segregation.. Limitations: The ductility of the NbMoTaW HEA at room temperature remains low, and while composition deviation exists (up to 3.5%), it is noted that further study of mechanical properties is still necessary.. Future work: Further study of mechanical properties is required to fully assess the potential of the SLM-fabricated NbMoTaW HEA.. Quote: "The HEA shows an excellent microstructure, microhardness, and corrosion resistance performance compared with traditional superalloys."

card: Paper card. Question: How does varying tungsten concentration affect the crystal structure, microstructure, and mechanical properties (hardness, strength, ductility) of WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys fabricated via laser cladding deposition?. System: WxNbMoTa refractory high-entropy alloys with x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53 (mole fractions). Processing: Laser cladding deposition (LCD) using a coaxial LCD system with 565 W laser power, 8 mm/s scanning speed, 0.08 mm layer thickness, and 600 °C induction heating temperature; powders (45–125 μm) mixed for 4 h and dried at 120 °C for 8 h in Argon (<80 ppm O2). Test conditions: Vickers microhardness (500 g load, 30 s); room temperature compression (25 °C, 0.001 s⁻¹); high-temperature compression (1000 °C, 3.5 min heating, 15 min soak, 0.001 s⁻¹ strain rate, 10⁻³ torr vacuum). Findings: All WxNbMoTa alloys formed a single-phase body-centered cubic (BCC) solid solution regardless of tungsten content.; Grain and dendrite sizes averaged 20 μm and 4 μm, respectively, due to rapid solidification in LCD.; Vickers microhardness increased with tungsten concentration: 459.2 ± 9.7, 476.0 ± 12.9, 485.3 ± 8.7, and 497.6 ± 5.6 Hv for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; NbMoTa (x = 0) exhibited yield strength of 530 MPa and compressive strain of 8.5% at 1000 °C.; At room temperature, NbMoTa showed yield strength of 874 MPa and compressive strain of 5.8%, while W-containing alloys were brittle with compressive strengths of 840–895 MPa.; Bulk modulus increased with tungsten content: 174, 182, 186, and 192 GPa for x = 0, 0.16, 0.33, 0.53.; Spherical gas porosities in as-fabricated samples were eliminated by using molybdenum powders with higher granule density and good sphericity.. Mechanism: Rapid solidification during laser cladding deposition (melting in 10⁻³–10⁻² s) suppresses constitutional segregation and promotes fine equiaxed grains. Tungsten addition increases lattice distortion and solid solution strengthening, raising hardness and bulk modulus but reducing ductility at room temperature. Porosity formation is attributed to adsorbed Argon gas in low-density molybdenum powder particles, not microstructure features.. Limitations: Spherical gas porosities appeared in samples fabricated with standard molybdenum powders due to low granule density; tungsten addition reduces room-temperature plasticity, making W-containing alloys brittle.. Future work: The present work provides a theoretical basis for LCD manufacturing of aerospace parts of refractory HEAs with large size, complex structure, and variable composition.. Quote: "The size of the grains and dendrites are 20 μm and 4 μm on average, due to the rapid solidification characteristics of the laser cladding deposition."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the presence of local chemical order (LCO) influence the formation, evolution, and recombination of irradiation-induced point defects and defect clusters in equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloys compared to a random solid solution?. System: Equiatomic CrCoNi medium-entropy alloy (MEA) in two states: water-quenched (approximated as a random solid solution, RSS) and aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h (LCO CrCoNi); pure Ni used as a benchmark.. Processing: Raw ingot homogenized at 1,200 °C for 48 h; split into two treatments: (1) water quenched to room temperature to form RSS; (2) aged at 1,000 °C for 120 h followed by slow furnace cooling to induce LCO. Ion irradiation performed in situ at 300 K using 50 keV He+ ions. Atomistic simulations prepared RSS by random distribution and LCO via MD/MC at 1,300 K with variance-constrained semigrand canonical ensemble.. Test conditions: In situ TEM irradiation at 300 K with 50 keV He+ ions up to 1.0 dpa; MD simulations of primary damage with PKA energies of 5, 10, 20, and 40 keV; diffusion simulations at various temperatures (including 1,200 K) to measure vacancy and interstitial mobility.. Findings: The areal fraction of LCO regions is approximately 3% in water-quenched RSS CrCoNi versus ~30% in the 1,000 °C-aged LCO CrCoNi.; At a low irradiation dose of 0.16 dpa, the LCO sample is nearly defect-free while the RSS sample already contains visible defect clusters.; The number density of defect clusters in the LCO sample is significantly smaller than in the RSS sample across the entire dose range of 0.16 to 1.0 dpa.; The average activation energy for interstitial diffusion increases from 0.22 eV in RSS to 0.34 eV in LCO, while for vacancies it increases from 0.69 eV to 0.76 eV.; The difference in activation energy between interstitial and vacancy diffusion narrows from 0.47 eV in RSS to 0.42 eV in LCO, reducing the mobility ratio.; The correlation factor for interstitial diffusion decreases by 29% (from 0.232 to 0.165) in LCO compared to RSS, indicating stronger localization of interstitial motion.; Large-sized defect clusters (Ncluster > 30) are suppressed in LCO CrCoNi, with the number of point defects in large clusters being ~35% lower than in RSS.; The recombination rate of Frenkel pairs at the end of the thermal spike is nearly identical for RSS and LCO (~99.6%), but the LCO sample retains fewer surviving FPs due to enhanced recombination during the cooling phase.. Mechanism: The authors argue that LCO enhances irradiation resistance through a two-pronged kinetic effect: (1) it increases migration energy barriers, slowing down the diffusion of both vacancies and interstitials (localizing their motion); and (2) it narrows the mobility ratio between interstitials and vacancies (by affecting interstitials more strongly), which increases the probability of their recombination and annihilation during the cooling phase of the collision cascade, thereby reducing the number of surviving defects and large clusters.. Limitations: The study notes that small-sized defect clusters (Ncluster < 8) are not detectable by in-situ TEM due to resolution limits and are susceptible to dissolution, so the comparison between experiment and simulation focuses on large-sized clusters. The extent of LCO investigated is limited to chemical short-range order (CSRO) developed via the specific aging treatment.. Future work: The authors propose that tailoring composition and heat treatment to extend LCO beyond CSRO into medium-range or long-range order, or adding interstitial alloying elements (such as C, N) with chemical affinity for specific constituents, could further boost irradiation tolerance.. Quote: "increased local chemical order (e.g., via thermal aging) significantly enhances their resistance to irradiation damage by narrowing the mobility ratio of irradiation-induced interstitials and vacancies that can facilitate their recombination."

card: Paper card. Question: How does increasing chemical disorder and compositional complexity in single-phase concentrated solid solution alloys (SP-CSAs) affect energy dissipation pathways and subsequent defect evolution under ion irradiation?. System: Single-phase fcc concentrated solid solution alloys: elemental Nickel (Ni), binary NiCo, binary NiFe, and quaternary NiCoFeCr (all equiatomic), plus non-equiatomic Ni0.65Fe0.35 and Ni0.40Fe0.60.. Processing: High-purity elemental metals arc melted and drop cast into copper moulds; single crystals directionally solidified in an optical floating zone furnace under Ar atmosphere; polished to damage-free surfaces for ion channelling.. Test conditions: Room temperature irradiation using 3 MeV Au2+ ions (fluence 1-2 × 10^13 cm^-2) and 1.5 MeV Ni+ ions (fluence 6 × 10^13 to 2 × 10^14 cm^-2); electrical resistivity measured between 5 K and 300 K; thermal conductivity measured at room temperature; in situ ion channelling and high-resolution TEM characterization.. Findings: Electrical resistivity at 5 K increases from ~0.1 μΩ cm for Ni to 77.1 μΩ cm for NiCoFeCr, indicating a substantial reduction in electron mean free path.; Total thermal conductivity at 300 K decreases from 88 W m−1 K−1 for Ni to 12.8 W m−1 K−1 for NiCoFeCr.; Backscattering yield (damage indicator) for NiFe is approximately half that of pure Ni after 3 MeV Au irradiation.; Stable defect production in NiFe is ~2 times lower than in pure Ni according to molecular dynamics cascade simulations.; Quaternary NiCoFeCr shows ~5 times less accumulated damage than pure Ni under Ni ion irradiation.; Increasing Fe concentration from 35% to 60% in Ni-Fe alloys enhances irradiation resistance.; Stacking fault tetrahedra (SFT) sizes are smaller in alloys (4.3-4.4 nm) compared to pure Ni (7.0 nm) due to slower defect migration.. Mechanism: Chemical disorder in SP-CSAs causes significant smearing of the electronic band structure (Bloch spectral function), reducing the electron mean free path and drastically lowering electronic thermal conductivity. This leads to less efficient heat dissipation, prolonging the lifetime of thermal spikes generated by ion collisions. The extended thermal spike duration and localized energy deposition alter defect energetics, increasing migration barriers and formation energies, which suppresses the clustering of point defects into larger, deleterious structures.. Limitations: The study focuses on simple fcc lattice structures and early-stage defect dynamics; the authors note that the results should not be interpreted as HEAs being intrinsically more radiation resistant in all cases, but rather that complexity is a tunable parameter for modifying transport properties.. Future work: The authors propose further exploration to understand how chemistry and composition can alter energy dissipation mechanisms to drive self-recovery from damage states, aiming to design radiation-resistant alloys by controlling coupling strengths and defect energetics at the atomic and electronic levels.. Quote: "much slower energy dissipation results in less deleterious defects and consequent slower damage accumulation under ion irradiation."

card: Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) affect the mobility mechanisms of screw and edge dislocations in the MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) across a wide temperature range?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), specifically comparing random solid solution (RSS) and equilibrium SRO states at 800 K. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a moment tensor potential (MTP) machine-learning interatomic potential; SRO states equilibrated via hybrid MD/Monte Carlo (MD/MC) approach at 800 K. Test conditions: Temperatures from 300 K to 2000 K; applied shear stresses ranging from 0 to 3.0 GPa for screws and 0 to 1.0 GPa for edges; dislocation line length ~15 nm. Findings: At 300 K, SRO provides an extra strengthening of ~180 MPa for screw dislocations due to the formation of diffuse antiphase boundaries (DAPBs).; The strengthening effect of SRO on screw dislocations attenuates with increasing temperature, becoming negligible at 2000 K where mobility curves for RSS and SRO samples overlap.; A cross-slip locking mechanism involving the formation of jogs is observed for screw dislocations, providing extra strengthening independent of SRO presence.; Unlike screw dislocations, the mobility of edge dislocations is enhanced by the presence of SRO, particularly in the high-stress regime.; The SRO-induced enhancement of edge dislocation mobility extends to a characteristic length scale of approximately 1.2 nm into neighboring planes.; At 300 K, dislocation velocities in the MoNbTaW RHEA are significantly lower than in pure Mo and Nb, but this difference diminishes at 2000 K.; The attenuation of SRO strengthening at high temperatures is attributed to the increasing contribution of the entropy term (ΔS_kp) to the kink-pair formation free energy.. Mechanism: For screw dislocations, SRO creates an energy barrier (DAPB formation energy) that must be overcome during kink-pair nucleation, causing strengthening that is thermally activated and thus diminishes at high temperatures. For edge dislocations, SRO flattens the energy landscape, reducing solute drag effects and enhancing mobility despite the energy cost of disrupting order on the slip plane. Cross-slip locking in screws involves the formation of jogs on different slip planes that pin the dislocation line.. Limitations: The simulations use short dislocation line lengths (~15 nm) compared to realistic experimental conditions, meaning calculated velocities are dependent on this size and cannot be directly compared to macroscopic theoretical models without extrapolation. The study assumes the SRO state remains fixed during dislocation motion and does not account for changes in ordering around the moving core.. Future work: The authors state that predicting how the identified mechanisms combine to determine material strength requires appealing to mesoscale models for longer dislocation lengths and longer timescales, which is beyond the scope of the current work.. Quote: "The mobility of edge dislocations is found to be enhanced by the presence of SRO, whereas the rate of double-kink nucleation in the motion of screw dislocations is reduced."

Paper card. Question: How does chemical short-range order (SRO) and temperature affect the mobility and friction stress of edge versus screw dislocations in a bcc MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) compared to pure bcc metals and binary alloys?. System: MoNbTaW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA), pure Mo, and binary Mo-Nb alloys (Mo95Nb5 to Mo75Nb25). Processing: Machine-learning interatomic potential (MTP) with radius cutoff (Rcut) of 4.7 Å and maximum level (levmax) of 14; MC/MD equilibration at 800 K; dislocation mobility simulations using LAMMPS with shear stress ramped at 20 MPa per 1.5 ps and held for 150 ps at temperatures of 300 K and 2000 K. Test conditions: Temperatures: 300 K and 2000 K; Shear stress ramp rate: 20 MPa per 1.5 ps; Hold time: 150 ps; Critical friction stress defined at 0.2 Å/ps for screw and 1.0 Å/ps for edge dislocations. Findings: The edge-to-screw velocity ratio decreases from 20 at 300 K to 11 at 2000 K in MoNbTaW.; Critical friction stress for edge dislocations decreases by 140 MPa from 300 to 2000 K.; Critical friction stress for screw dislocations decreases by 1.3 GPa (an order of magnitude larger) from 300 to 2000 K.; At ~2000 K, the critical friction stresses for both edge and screw dislocations decay to approximately the same level.; SRO hinders screw dislocation motion but accelerates edge dislocation motion in the RHEA.; A novel cross-slip locking mechanism was observed in the RHEA, attributed to intrinsic energy fluctuations and rugged energy landscapes.; Critical stress for screw dislocations follows an exponential decay with temperature, while edge dislocations follow a linear decrease.; Binary Mo-Nb alloys show lower critical friction stresses compared to the RHEA, with edge friction converging to zero in pure bcc metals.. Mechanism: Screw dislocations move via kink-pair nucleation and migration; SRO increases the free-energy barrier for kink-pair nucleation, causing temperature-dependent strengthening. Edge dislocations are accelerated by SRO through the attenuation of solute interaction magnitudes. The cross-slip locking mechanism arises from intrinsic energy fluctuations along the dislocation line and the rugged energy landscape.. Limitations: The study notes that the cross-slip locking mechanism was observed even with a limited cell size, implying potential size effects, and the phenomenological model is constructed specifically for the double-kink mechanism.. Future work: The authors state that the findings demonstrate mechanisms that can have a significant impact on mechanical properties, implying future work should explore these impacts, though no specific future experiments are explicitly detailed in the provided text.. Quote: "The edge-to-screw mobility ratio is around 20 at 300 K, which decreases to 11 when the temperature is raised to 2000 K."

Question: What are the atomic-level mechanisms responsible for the high radiation damage tolerance and slower damage accumulation in the CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy compared to pure Ni and pure Fe?. System: CoCrFeMnNi high-entropy alloy (HEA), pure FCC Ni, and pure BCC Fe. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with a 2NN MEAM interatomic potential; displacement cascade simulation at 773 K with 10 keV PKA energy and 35 ps duration; defect evolution simulation at 773 K with 1 at% Frenkel pairs for 5 ns. Test conditions: Temperature: 773 K; PKA energy: 10 keV; PKA directions: <135> and <235>; Defect concentration: 1 at% Frenkel pairs; Simulation time: 35 ps (cascade) and 5 ns (evolution). Findings: The CoCrFeMnNi HEA has fewer residual defects after cascade simulation than pure Ni and pure Fe, despite having more peak defects.; Defect clusters in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA are unstable and do not transform into stable dislocation-containing clusters even after 15 ns of additional evolution.; The SIA migration energy in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA is much higher than in pure Ni and pure Fe.; The vacancy migration energy in the HEA is similar to the SIA migration energy, unlike pure Ni where they differ significantly.; The minimum threshold displacement energy in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA is relatively smaller than that of pure Ni and pure Fe.; Cascade propagation in the HEA is non-directional and confined to a limited space, preventing subcascade formation.; The fraction of remaining defects after evolution is smaller in the HEA compared to pure systems due to higher recombination probability.. Mechanism: The high radiation damage tolerance originates from lattice distortion due to alloy complexity, which causes high SIA migration energy and non-directional cascade propagation, confining defects to a limited space and increasing recombination. Additionally, the instability of defect clusters in the HEA prevents the formation of stable, immobile dislocation loops, allowing defects to remain as mobile single defects or small clusters that recombine easily.. Limitations: The displacement cascade simulation analyzing one recoil may not be sufficient to estimate radiation damage tolerance; the threshold displacement energy in the HEA cannot be uniquely defined at 0 K due to environmental variety; short-range repulsion in the potential for pure Co and Mn required minimal adjustment.. Future work: The authors suggest that similar improvement in radiation resistance can be generally expected in various multi-principal element alloys due to the lattice distortion caused by chemical complexity.. Quote: "The defect clusters appearing in the CoCrFeMnNi HEA after the defect evolution are unstable because of the alloy complexity."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the morphology of CeO2 supports influence hydrogen spillover to enable the synthesis of sub-nanometer high-entropy alloy (HEA) clusters, and what are the resulting catalytic properties and structural reversibility under oxidative/reductive conditions?. System: CoNiCuZnPd HEA clusters supported on CeO2 nanorods (CeO2-NRs), CeO2 nanocubes (CeO2-NCs), and CeO2 nanoparticles (CeO2-NPs). Processing: Hydrothermal synthesis of CeO2 supports (NRs at 90°C for 24h, NCs at 180°C); impregnation of metal precursors (Co:Ni:Cu:Zn:Pd = 1:1:1:1:1) onto CeO2; reduction under H2 flow at 600°C without calcination. Test conditions: NO reduction by H2 (50–200°C); H/D exchange (300°C D2, then -50°C to 200°C H2); in situ XAFS under 8000 ppm NO/He and 20,000 ppm H2/He at 400°C. Findings: CeO2-NRs with exposed (110) facets produced the most intense HD peak in H/D exchange, exceeding CeO2-NPs and CeO2-NCs by factors of 2.6 and 4.4, respectively.; CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs formed sub-nanometer clusters with an estimated diameter of 0.79 nm (average of 13 atoms) and a coordination number of 5.6.; The CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs catalyst achieved 100% NO conversion at 100°C, significantly lower than NPs (150°C) and NCs (200°C).; In situ XANES showed the Pd0 fraction in CoNiCuZnPd/CeO2-NRs remained at 0.78 after 30 min NO exposure, compared to 0.37 for monometallic Pd/CeO2-NRs.; FT-EXAFS revealed that under NO, short Pd–M bonds (2.1 Å) disappeared and long Pd–Pd bonds appeared, indicating sacrificial oxidation of non-noble metals.; DFT calculations showed NO adsorption energy on the HEA cluster was higher than on monometallic slabs, while H adsorption energy remained comparable.; The HEA13(Co2Ni2Cu3Zn3Pd3) cluster model reproduced a unique flat XANES post-edge shape, confirming the sub-nanometer solid-solution structure.. Mechanism: Hydrogen spillover on reducible (110) facets of CeO2-NRs facilitates simultaneous proton-electron transfer, reducing metal cations with different potentials at low temperatures to form sub-nanometer HEA clusters. Under oxidative conditions, non-noble metals undergo sacrificial oxidation to form oxide shells around Pd cores (Pd@MOx), suppressing Pd oxidation and enabling structural reversibility upon reduction.. Limitations: The text notes that synthesis of sub-nanometer HEA clusters remains challenging and that CeO2-NCs and CeO2-NPs resulted in phase-segregated or larger nanoparticles rather than uniform sub-nanometer clusters.. Future work: Further extension, including the detailed optimization of the components as well as their ratio, is under investigation.. Quote: "The CoNiCuZnPd HEA sub-nanoclusters exhibited higher activity during the reduction of NO by H2 even at low temperatures compared with the corresponding monometallic catalysts."

Test conditions: 50 mL/min flow of a NO/H2/He mixture containing 8000 ppm NO and 20,000 ppm H2; 50 mg quantity of catalyst in a quartz cell with an internal diameter of 4 mm.
