card: Paper card. Question: How can the miscibility gap in bimetallic Co-Mo alloys be overcome to create tunable, highly active catalysts for ammonia decomposition using earth-abundant elements?. System: Quinary CoMoFeNiCu high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (general composition CoxMoyFe10Ni10Cu10 where x + y = 70) and control samples of bimetallic Co-Mo and monometallic Ru. Processing: Carbothermal shock technique involving flash heating and cooling of metal precursors on oxygenated carbon nanofibers; temperature reached 2000–2300 K with ramping rates on the order of 10^5 K s−1 and shock duration of ~55 ms. Test conditions: Ammonia decomposition in a plug flow reactor at 250–600 °C using 5 vol% NH3 (and 100 vol% NH3 for specific tests) at a gas hourly space velocity (GHSV) of 36 L gcat−1 h−1. Findings: HEA-Co25Mo45 achieved a mass-specific reaction rate of 22.1 gNH3 gmetals−1 h−1 at 500 °C, representing an improvement factor of ~19 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~3 versus Ru.; The most active catalyst, HEA-Co25Mo45, reached 50% NH3 conversion (T50) at 422 °C, compared to 600 °C for Ru and 600 °C for bimetallic Co-Mo.; The apparent activation energy (Eapp) varied from 64.7 kJ mol−1 for the most active HEA-Co25Mo45 to 123.1 kJ mol−1 for the least active HEA-Co55Mo15.; Nitrogen desorption energy (ΔEN) for HEA-Co25Mo45 was ~79 kJ mol−1, which is very close to the value for Ru (84 kJ mol−1).; Catalytic activity exhibited a volcano-type behavior with respect to nitrogen adsorption energy, peaking at an optimal ΔEN of ~79 kJ mol−1.; The HEA-Co25Mo45 catalyst showed negligible degradation after ~50 hours of continuous operation at 500 °C.; For pure NH3 decomposition, HEA-Co55Mo15 achieved an improvement factor of ~118 versus bimetallic Co-Mo and ~40 versus Ru.; Atomistic modeling confirmed a single solid-solution phase with δ = 5.4% and ΔHmix = 0.65 kJ mol−1, showing no phase segregation up to 1000 K.. Mechanism: The high catalytic activity is attributed to the robust tuning of surface nitrogen binding strength via the Co/Mo ratio; the optimal activity arises from a tradeoff where Co-rich catalysts bind N too weakly (limiting dehydrogenation) and Mo-rich catalysts bind N too strongly (limiting N2 desorption), with the HEA composition allowing access to the optimal intermediate binding energy (~79 kJ mol−1) predicted by the Sabatier principle.. Limitations: The text notes that the peak intensities in XRD patterns are low due to the much smaller particle sizes compared to previously reported HEAs, and that the bimetallic Co-Mo catalysts are constrained by large miscibility gaps in their phase diagram.. Future work: The authors propose designing practical reactors with cascaded catalyst layers having gradually changing nitrogen binding strengths to match the varying concentration of NH3 along the flow, which can be readily achieved by varying the Co/Mo ratios in HEA catalysts.. Quote: "Quinary CoMoFeNiCu nanoparticles are synthesized in a single solid-solution phase with robust control over the Co/Mo atomic ratio, including those ratios considered to be immiscible according to the Co-Mo bimetallic phase diagram."

card: Paper card. Question: How can uniformly dispersed high-entropy alloy nanoparticles (HEA-NPs) be synthesized on granular supports (e.g., carbon, Al2O3, zeolite) without phase separation, overcoming the limitations of conventional fixed-bed pyrolysis?. System: Denary (MnCoNiCuRhPdSnIrPtAu), quinary (FeCoPdIrPt, CuPdSnPtAu), and other multi-element (up to 10 elements) HEA-NPs supported on graphene oxide (GO), carbon black, γ-Al2O3, and zeolite (Permutit). Processing: Fast moving bed pyrolysis (FMBP) following wet impregnation: Metal chlorides coordinated with 1,10-Phenanthroline loaded on supports; quartz boat pushed into a 923 K furnace zone at 20 cm s−1 (reaching 923 K within 5 s); annealing for 120 min at 923 K under Ar (100 sccm) or H2 (100 sccm) for oxide supports. Test conditions: Electrochemical hydrogen evolution reaction (HER) in 1 M KOH (pH 13.8) at 10 mA cm−2 and 100 mA cm−2; stability tested via chronopotentiometry for 150 h; structural characterization via HR-STEM, HAADF-STEM, EDX, XRD, XPS, and ICP-OES. Findings: HEA-NPs achieved a narrow size distribution of ~2 nm up to denary compositions at 923 K; FMBP ensures simultaneous pyrolysis of mixed precursors, preventing phase separation unlike fixed-bed pyrolysis (FBP) which yields phase-separated alloys; FeCoPdIrPt@GO exhibited an overpotential of 42 mV at 10 mA cm−2, lower than commercial Pt/C (64 mV); Mass activity of FeCoPdIrPt@GO at 100 mV overpotential was 9.1 mA μgPt, 26 times higher than Pt/C (0.35 mA μgPt); Long-term stability of 150 h maintained at 10 mA cm−2 with no obvious change in morphology or composition; Atomic ratio error in synthesized alloys was below 15%, confirmed by EDX and ICP-OES; Tafel slope for FeCoPdIrPt was 82 mV dec−1, indicating the fastest kinetics among tested samples. Mechanism: The rapid heating to 923 K within 5 s creates high supersaturation of monomers, leading to a small critical nucleus radius (r* = 0.313 nm) and low critical excess free energy (ΔGr* = 2.54 × 10−20 J). This thermodynamically favors the formation of small, homogeneous nuclei clusters without phase separation, whereas slower heating (FBP/SMBP) results in larger nuclei and phase segregation due to higher ΔGr*.. Limitations: The text notes that HEA-NPs with low loading (3 wt%) were too small for clear EDX mapping, requiring higher loading (10 wt%) for elemental analysis; also, annealing times of 30 min led to carbon wrapping, while 180 min caused significant particle growth.. Future work: The authors propose a scalable method for production of supported HEA-NPs and suggest the strategy opens a venue for synthesizing alloys with tunable compositions for applications in catalysis, chemical sensing, biology, and energy conversion.. Quote: "Fast moving bed pyrolysis strategy ensures the mixed metal precursors rapidly and simultaneously pyrolyzed at high temperatures, resulting in nuclei with a small size."
W3020204536.title: Synthesis of high-entropy alloy nanoparticles on supports by the fast moving bed pyrolysis

card: Paper card. Question: How can high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanoparticles be synthesized at low temperatures on conventional supports, and what mechanisms govern their formation and catalytic performance in CO2 hydrogenation?. System: CoNiCuRuPd high-entropy alloy nanoparticles supported on TiO2 (CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2); comparison with CoNiCuRuPd/Al2O3, CoNiCuRuPd/MgO, and monometallic Pd/TiO2, Ru/TiO2, Co/TiO2, Ni/TiO2, Cu/TiO2. Processing: Simple impregnation of TiO2 with aqueous solutions of Co(NO3)2·6H2O, Ni(NO3)2·6H2O, Cu(NO3)2·3H2O, RuCl3·nH2O, and Na2PdCl4 (1:1:1:1:1 molar ratio; Pd 1.0 wt%); reduction under H2 flow (20 mL/min) at 400 °C for 2 h without prior calcination. Test conditions: CO2 hydrogenation at atmospheric pressure, 300–400 °C, with N2/H2/CO2 mixture (4/5/1 composition, total flow 50 mL/min, SV = 6000 mL/g/h); stability tested over 72 h; in situ XAFS and XRD under H2 at 200–400 °C; H2-TPR from 50 to 600 °C at 5 °C/min; CO-TPD and FTIR; TEM/STEM/EDX; ETEM under 300 kV electron beam; DFT and MD simulations at 900 K. Findings: CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 nanoparticles achieved an average size of 1.90 nm with a single-phase fcc structure (lattice parameter a = 3.734 Å), whereas CoNiCuRuPd/Al2O3 and CoNiCuRuPd/MgO yielded larger (6.65 and 6.73 nm), partially segregated particles.; The quinary-component precursors on TiO2 showed a single H2-TPR reduction peak at ~170 °C, indicating simultaneous reduction of all five metal ions, unlike broad peaks (130–250 °C) on Al2O3 and MgO.; CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 exhibited 2–13 times higher yield of hydrogenated products than MgO and Al2O3 supports, with 68.3% CH4 selectivity at 400 °C.; The apparent activation energy for CO2 hydrogenation on CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 was 37.7 kJ/mol, lower than 44.2 kJ/mol for Pd/TiO2.; After 72 h of reaction, CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 retained 96% of its initial activity, while Pd/TiO2 dropped to 76% and Ru/TiO2 to 89%.; Particle growth was suppressed in CoNiCuRuPd/TiO2 (final diameter 2.3 nm) compared to Pd/TiO2 (final diameter 5.3 nm) after 72 h.; DFT calculations showed the cohesive energy of the HEA cluster (−3.92 eV) was higher than that of a pure Pd cluster (−3.09 eV), and diffusion coefficients in the HEA were ~1/3 lower than in pure Pd at 900 K.; CO adsorption on the HEA surface was stronger (Ead = −37.5 kcal/mol) than on pure Pd (−26.2 kcal/mol), shifting the CO stretching frequency from 2091 cm−1 (Pd/TiO2) to 2070 cm−1 (HEA/TiO2) and delaying desorption to >150 °C.. Mechanism: The formation is driven by hydrogen spillover on TiO2: Pd2+ precursors are first reduced to form Pd nuclei; H2 dissociates on Pd to form Pd–H species; protons and electrons transfer to TiO2 lattice O2− anions, generating mobile H atoms that migrate rapidly over TiO2 via coupled proton/electron transfer, reducing all metal precursors simultaneously to form a solid-solution HEA. The sluggish diffusion and lattice distortion in the HEA enhance durability, while the cocktail effect (synergistic electronic properties) improves catalytic activity and CH4 selectivity by strengthening CO adsorption.. Limitations: The study notes that the synthesis method was demonstrated only for the CoNiCuRuPd system and a few preliminary tests with Rh, Pt, and Au; applicability to other compositions requires further investigation. The text also mentions that monometallic Ru/TiO2 showed high activity but attributed it to extremely small particle size (0.89 nm), implying size effects must be controlled when comparing HEAs to monometallics.. Future work: The authors state that 'Further investigation to demonstrate the applicability of the present synthetic method is now under investigation' for other metal combinations (e.g., Rh, Pt, Au) and suggest the approach offers 'advanced insights into an innovative catalyst/photocatalyst architecture providing an essentially unlimited compositional space.'. Quote: "This process is driven by the pronounced hydrogen spillover effect on TiO2 in conjunction with coupled proton/electron transfer."

card: Paper card. Question: How do the proportions of high-density elements Hf and Ta affect the mechanical properties (strength, elastic modulus, dislocation density) of Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, and can a low-density composition be successfully formed via laser melting deposition (LMD) to overcome microstructural coarsening?. System: Hf-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr high-entropy alloys, specifically HfxNbTaxTiZr (x = 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1) and the designed low-density Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr. Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using LAMMPS with NPT system relaxation and strain rate of 4 × 10^8 s^-1; Experimental preparation via arc melting for as-cast samples and Laser Melting Deposition (LMD) using a 3 kW semiconductor laser (wavelength 900–1070 nm), laser power 600–1400 W, scanning rate 4 mm/s, powder feeding rate 8 g/min, and height increment 0.5 mm. Test conditions: Room temperature tensile testing at a constant displacement speed of 0.3 mm/min; XRD analysis (10~90° 2θ, 10°/min); SEM and EBSD for microstructure; Vickers hardness testing. Findings: MD simulations show that decreasing the Ta element proportion reduces the yield strength of the HEA.; Decreasing the Hf element proportion increases the yield strength of the HEA.; Simultaneously decreasing Hf and Ta ratios reduces the elastic modulus and strength, leading to microstructure coarsening in as-cast samples.; LMD processing refines the grain size of Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr from 300 μm (as-cast) to 20–80 μm (as-deposited).; The as-deposited Hf0.25NbTa0.25TiZr HEA exhibits a yield strength (σs) of 925 ± 9 MPa, compared to 730 ± 23 MPa for the as-cast version.; The as-deposited low-density alloy achieves strength similar to the as-cast equiatomic HfNbTaTiZr HEA (σs = 970 ± 15 MPa).; The as-deposited microstructure shows an alternating distribution of coarse columnar grains and fine equiaxed grains along the z-direction.; Dislocation density in the as-deposited alloy is higher than in as-cast samples due to thermal stress accumulation during LMD.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the strength increase in as-deposited samples to grain refinement and the Hall-Petch relation, where grain boundaries resist slip transfer. The coarsening in as-cast low-Hf/Ta alloys is explained by the reduction in these elements. The formation of columnar grains in LMD is caused by epitaxial growth from successive thermal cycles, while equiaxed grains form due to lower nucleation barriers, reducing anisotropy. Increased mechanical properties in LMD samples are also linked to the accumulation of thermal stress increasing dislocation density.. Limitations: The MD simulation model scale is too small to accurately reflect the effect of grain boundaries and grain size on alloy properties, leading to quantitative differences between simulated and actual values.. Future work: The authors suggest that while MD simulation has quantitative limitations, its qualitative analysis reduces the amount of experiments needed in component design, and combining it with additive manufacturing technology has good application prospects for engineering.. Quote: "The simultaneous decrease in the ratio of Hf and Ta elements reduces the elastic modulus and strength of HEA and leads to the coarsening of the alloy microstructure."

card: Paper card. Question: What are the individual effects of Mo, Nb, Ta, Ti, and Zr on the microstructure and mechanical properties (yield strength, ductility, and elevated-temperature performance) of equiatomic Hf-Mo-Nb-Ta-Ti-Zr refractory high-entropy alloys?. System: Equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr and its five sub-alloys created by the subtraction method: HfNbTaTiZr, HfMoTaTiZr, HfMoNbTiZr, HfMoNbTaZr, and HfMoNbTaTi. Processing: Vacuum-arc melting of 99.9 wt.% (99.99 wt.% for Ti) pure elements stacked by melting point, re-melted at least four times, and solidified in a water-cool copper mold. Test conditions: Compression tests at room temperature, 800 °C, 1000 °C, 1200 °C, and 1400 °C; crosshead speed 0.36 mm/min (strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹); cylindrical samples 3.6 mm diameter x 6 mm height. Findings: HfMoNbTaTiZr alloy yield strength was 1512 MPa at room temperature and 556 MPa at 1200 °C.; HfMoTaTiZr (Nb removed) showed the highest room temperature yield strength of 1600 MPa but lower toughness.; HfMoNbTaTi (Zr removed) exhibited the best comprehensive properties with 27% fracture strain at room temperature and 367 MPa yield strength at 1400 °C.; The presence of Mo increased room temperature yield strength from 929 MPa (in HfNbTaTiZr) to 1512 MPa but reduced fracture strain from >50% to 12%.; Nb addition increased yield strength by 38% at 1200 °C and significantly improved room temperature fracture strain.; Zr addition increased strength but strongly deteriorated room temperature toughness, reducing fracture strain from 27% to 12%.; Alloys with Mo present showed much better strength at elevated temperatures compared to HfNbTaTiZr.; At 1200 °C, HfMoNbTaTi alloy had the highest specific strength among the tested alloys.. Mechanism: The high yield strength is attributed to the solid solution strengthening effect driven by atomic size and shear modulus mismatch; the high entropy effect promotes the formation of a single BCC disordered solid solution phase despite binary phase diagrams suggesting intermetallics; severe lattice distortion reduces the effective shear modulus by approximately 30% compared to the rule of mixtures.. Limitations: There is a deviation of about 30% between calculated and experimental yield strengths, likely due to overestimated shear modulus; the criteria for Laves phase formation were not fully consistent with experimental observations; the reduction in shear modulus due to lattice distortion requires further research to confirm reasons.. Future work: Further modification of composition and/or anti-oxidation coatings are required for high-temperature applications in air; more research is needed to confirm the elemental effects in other RHEA systems and to understand the reasons for reduced shear modulus.. Quote: "The subtraction method was applied on equiatomic HfMoNbTaTiZr alloys to discover the role of each element"

card: Paper card. Question: Can a hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (MC/MD) simulation methodology realistically predict the nanometer-level local structural features, short-range clustering (SRC) morphology, and thermodynamic aspects of a Ta-Nb-Hf-Zr high-entropy alloy without manual experimental input?. System: Equimolar Ta0.25Nb0.25Hf0.25Zr0.25 high-entropy alloy (HEA). Processing: Created a 11664-atom bcc supercell (18×18×18) with random atomic assignment; performed NPT simulation at 2073 K to determine lattice parameter (3.54 Å); subjected to hybrid MC/MD evolution at 1800 °C with 583,200 attempted swaps (50 swaps/atom) using EAM potentials and conjugate gradient energy minimization.. Test conditions: Simulated annealing at 1800 °C (2073 K); validation against experimental HRTEM (4 days annealing), APT, and synchrotron X-ray diffraction data.. Findings: The simulated structure evolved from a random solid solution to form Zr and Hf-rich short-range clusters (SRCs) after approximately 15 MC swaps.; The width of the SRCs obtained from MC/MD simulation was close to 1–1.2 nm, matching the 1–1.5 nm width measured by APT.; The energy of the evolving structure reduced rapidly by 60 m eV/atom within the first 10 MC swaps and by 80 m eV/atom by 15 MC swaps.; The SRCs grew perpendicular to the <1 0 0> crystallographic directions, forming an interconnected grid-like pattern after 25 MC swaps.; The elastic anisotropy factor (A) calculated from the MD simulation was between 2.15 and 2.26, indicating lower elastic strain energy along <1 0 0> directions.; Simulated X-ray diffraction patterns showed streak-like diffuse scattering along <1 0 0> directions that matched experimental observations in both asymmetry and thickness.; The simulated system size of approximately 6.4 nm was comparable to the 10 nm coherent domain size determined from neutron diffraction experiments.. Mechanism: The formation of SRCs in the {1 0 0} habit planes and the associated local structural relaxation are attributed to the elastic anisotropy of the matrix (A > 1), which promotes the growth of Zr and Hf-rich clusters along directions of lower elastic strain energy, causing tetragonal lattice expansion relaxations due to the larger atomic volumes of Zr and Hf.. Limitations: The study notes that previous DFT-based MC/MD studies were limited to tiny structures (128–256 atoms) due to high computational costs, and while this work uses classical MD, it relies on the accuracy of the developed EAM potential.. Future work: The authors propose that this MC/MD technique can greatly reduce the need for costly experimental characterizations (HRTEM, APT, synchrotron XRD) and accelerate the pace of materials development by reducing development cost and time.. Quote: "The structure evolution technique is based on a combined hybrid Monte Carlo and molecular dynamics (MC/MD) approach."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the feasibility of using a Si-20Cr-20Fe coating to improve the oxidation resistance of MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloys, and how do the microstructure and composition of the coating evolve during high-temperature oxidation?. System: MoNbTaTiW refractory high-entropy alloy (RHEA) substrate with a Si-20Cr-20Fe (wt.%) silicide coating. Processing: Fused slurry method: Si-20Cr-20Fe powder mixed with 4% polyethylene alcohol binder, applied to polished RHEA cuboids, dried at 80 °C, then vacuum annealed at 1430 °C for 1 h under 5 × 10−3 Pa. Test conditions: Oxidation in static air at 1000 °C and 1300 °C for 1 h with a heating rate of 10 °C/min. Findings: The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure with an outer MSi2 layer (66.2 at.% Si) and an inner M5Si3 layer (37.9 at.% Si).; The initial coating thickness was ~113 µm, increasing to 347 µm after oxidation at 1000 °C and 397 µm after oxidation at 1300 °C.; After oxidation at 1000 °C, the coating developed a three-layer structure (two silicide layers, one oxide layer) with a gap between the oxide and silicide layers.; After oxidation at 1300 °C, the coating developed a four-layer structure (two silicide layers, two oxide layers) with no gap between the oxide and silicide layers.; The outer oxide layer at 1000 °C consisted of SiO2, TiO2, Cr2SiO4, Ta0.3W0.7O2.85, and Ti0.67Nb1.33O4.; The outer oxide layer at 1300 °C consisted of CrNbO4, SiO2, WO3, and Fe2SiO4, with no Mo or Ta oxides detected.; Silicon diffused from the coating into the substrate, causing the silicide layer to move inward while its thickness increased significantly (e.g., L2 layer grew from 67 µm to 181 µm at 1000 °C).; The L1 layer (M5Si3) thickness decreased from ~46 µm to ~33 µm (1000 °C) and ~34 µm (1300 °C), while the L2 layer (MSi2) thickness more than doubled.. Mechanism: Silicon diffused from the silicide coating into the RHEA substrate during oxidation, causing the silicide layer to move toward the substrate and increase in thickness. The oxide layer formed on the surface, with its structure and composition depending on temperature; at 1300 °C, complete oxidation of metals and silicon, combined with the volatilization of oxides like MoO3, resulted in a stable oxide layer volume without gaps, whereas at 1000 °C, volume expansion caused bulging and gaps.. Limitations: The text does not explicitly state limitations of the study.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work.. Quote: "The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M5Si3 as the inner layer."

card: Paper card. Question: Can large tensile ductility be achieved at high-stress levels in metallic nanopillars, and what are the underlying deformation mechanisms enabling room-temperature super-elongation in high-entropy alloys?. System: Single-crystalline <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy (HEA) nanopillars; also compared with pure Al, Ni, Ag, Al0.1CoCrFeNi, and CoCrNi nanopillars. Processing: Bulk CoCrFeNi fabricated by arc melting equiatomic pure metal powders (>99.9% purity), homogenized at 1473 K for 24 h, cold rolled (65% reduction), and annealed at 1373 K for 1 h; nanopillars with ~350 nm length and ~70 nm width fabricated via focused ion beam (FIB) milling using 30 kV/300 pA and 50 pA beams, with final cleaning at 5 kV/100 pA; in situ tensile testing performed at room temperature with a strain rate of ~2.8 × 10−3 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature; uniaxial tensile loading along <100>, <110>, and <111> crystallographic directions; strain rate of ~2.8 × 10−3 s−1; in situ TEM and STEM characterization; large-scale molecular dynamics simulations at 300 K with strain rate of 5 × 108 s−1. Findings: Achieved uniform tensile elongation of ~110% at flow stresses of 0.6–1.0 GPa in <110>-oriented CoCrFeNi nanopillars at room temperature.; The <100> and <111> oriented nanopillars exhibited very limited plasticity due to shear localization and deformation twinning, respectively.; Deformation was mediated by spatial and synergistic coordination of deformation twinning and dislocation slip, with twin fraction reaching ~90% in simulations.; Nanoscale twins with an average thickness of ~1 nm nucleated, propagated, interacted, and coalesced, leading to lattice reorientation from <110> to <100>.; Detwinning and twin thickening occurred via partial dislocation emission from twin boundary (TB) and free surface intersections.; Generalized stacking fault energy (SFE) in CoCrFeNi showed substantial scattering (wide distribution) due to atomic-level compositional heterogeneities, unlike the fixed SFE in pure Ni.; Pure metal nanopillars (Al, Ni, Ag) showed lower elongation (~30% for Al/Ni, ~60% for Ag) with premature failure due to hindered twin propagation.; Critical twinning stress calculated to be 628–903 MPa, consistent with experimental yield strength range of 0.6–1.0 GPa.. Mechanism: The ultrahigh uniform tensile ductility arises from the spatial and synergistic activation of deformation twinning and dislocation slip, driven by atomic-level chemical compositional heterogeneities that create a wide spectrum of local stacking fault energies. This variability allows for persistent nucleation of partial dislocations and continuous twin propagation/coalescence, which delocalize plastic strain, suppress strain localization, and delay necking failure.. Limitations: The study notes that initial dislocation density and width-thickness ratio significantly influence dislocation density evolution but have weak influence on twin fraction evolution; the authors state that quantifying these influences further is needed. Additionally, the simulations used a high strain rate (5 × 108 s−1) compared to experiments, and the effect of short-range ordering (SRO) was found to slightly increase yield strength but not fundamentally alter the deformation mechanism.. Future work: The authors state: 'In the future, we will further quantify the influences of initial dislocation density, width-thickness ratio, and other configuration parameters (including sample shape/morphology and atomic ordering) on the evolutions of dislocation density and twin fraction, which is crucial for understanding the plastic deformation behaviors and mechanisms of HEAs.'. Quote: "unusual room-temperature uniform elongation up to ~110% at a high flow stress of 0.6–1.0 GPa"

card: Paper card. Question: How does high-strain deformation influence the transition between chemical clustering and ordering in an Al0.1CrCoFeNi high-entropy alloy, and what are the underlying mechanisms compared to tensile loading?. System: Al0.1CrCoFeNi (quinary high-entropy alloy with Al mole fraction x = 0.1). Processing: Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations using a derived EAM-LJ force-field; alloy melted at 2,200 K, quenched at 21.11 K/ps to 300 K, then deformed at a strain rate of 10^10 s^-1 under NPT/NVT/NVE ensembles. Test conditions: Compressive and tensile loading at temperatures of 77 K, 300 K, 700 K, and 1,000 K; strain rates of 10^10 s^-1; engineering strain up to 0.9%. Findings: A peak flow stress of ~125 MPa is recorded for compressive loading at 77 and 300 K, dropping to ~90 MPa at 700 and 1,000 K.; Under compressive loading, a clustering-to-ordering transition occurs with an increase in unlike pair correlations (e.g., Al-Co, Al-Cr) and a decrease in like pair correlations (e.g., Al-Al).; No strain hardening is observed under tensile deformation, whereas compressive loading shows marked evidence of strain hardening.; The Al-Ni pair possesses the strongest interchange-energy fluctuations at a long-wavelength (k = [000]), driving clustering behavior.; The calculated spinodal temperature (Tsp) is 840 K, which agrees with the experimentally-observed transition temperature of 813–823 K.; Large fluctuations in stress under compressive loading at elevated temperatures are attributed to thermo-plastic instability in the shear band.; The lattice parameter (a0) predicted by MD simulations is 3.55 Å at 0 K, in reasonable agreement with KKR-CPA (3.51–3.57 Å) and experiment (3.57 Å).. Mechanism: The authors attribute the clustering-to-ordering transition under compression to atomistic rearrangements at high strains, where the high-strain compression promotes the formation of unlike pairs. Conversely, tensile loading induces a plastic flow condition similar to wire-drawing, maintaining the clustering phase. The large fluctuations at high temperatures are caused by thermo-plastic instability leading to shear-induced disordering.. Limitations: The study notes that the high strain rates (~10^10 s^-1) chosen are due to length and time scale limitations in MD simulations and restrict the use of experimentally-realizable high strain rates (~10^2 s^-1). Additionally, the 'size effect' including local site displacements is not included in the linear-response (k;T) calculations.. Future work: The investigation provides further motivation for the experimental exploration of high-temperature compressive thermo-plastic instability in Al0.1CrCoFeNi.. Quote: "high-strain compression promotes atomistic rearrangements in Al0.1CrCoFeNi, resulting in a clustering-to-ordering transition that is absent for tensile loading."

card: Paper card. Question: What is the magnetic state that develops in the highly structurally and chemically inhomogeneous Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 single-crystalline high-entropy alloy?. System: Al28Co20Cr11Fe15Ni26 single-crystalline high-entropy alloy (ACCFN). Processing: Czochralski monocrystal growth from a heterogeneous tungsten seed under 650 mbar Ar atmosphere at a pulling rate of 1 mm/h. Test conditions: Direct-current magnetization, hysteresis curves, alternating-current magnetic susceptibility, and thermoremanent magnetization time decay measured from 1.8 to 400 K; magnetic fields up to 7 T and 100 mT; AC frequencies 1–1000 Hz. Findings: The material consists of a B2 matrix (94 vol%) and spherical A2 nanoparticles (6 vol%) with an average diameter of 64 nm.; The Cr-free B2 matrix (Al28Co25Fe15Ni32) forms a disordered ferromagnetic state with a Curie temperature TC ≈ 390 K.; The A2 nanoparticles (Co19Cr56Fe25) exhibit a core-shell structure with CoFe-enriched shells of ~2 nm thickness.; The nanoparticle shells are ferromagnetic, while the nanoparticle cores are asperomagnetic (a subclass of spin glasses).; Asperomagnetism in the nanoparticle cores develops below a spin-freezing temperature Tf ≈ 15 K.; Below 15 K, the system exhibits broken-ergodicity phenomena, including a growing difference between zero-field-cooled and field-cooled magnetizations.; The low-temperature M(H) curve at 1.8 K shows a linear tail at high fields, confirming a minor antiferromagnetic component from the asperomagnetic cores.; No mictomagnetic (cluster glass) state was observed, as zfc and fc hysteresis curves perfectly overlapped at 6 K.. Mechanism: The B2 matrix contains only ferromagnetic elements (Co, Fe, Ni) leading to a disordered ferromagnetic state with positive exchange interactions. The A2 nanoparticles contain the antiferromagnetic element Cr alongside Co and Fe, creating mixed FM/AFM interactions. This results in a distribution of exchange interactions where FM interactions dominate but AFM interactions exist, forming an asperomagnetic state in the cores. The core-shell structure arises from CoFe enrichment at the A2–B2 interfaces. The asperomagnetic state is magnetically frustrated, leading to ergodicity breaking and spin freezing below 15 K.. Limitations: The ferromagnetic nature of the nanoparticle shells could not be verified experimentally by bulk magnetization measurements because their signal is masked by the much stronger ferromagnetic contribution from the B2 matrix.. Quote: "The results reveal that the Cr-free B2 matrix of composition Al28Co25Fe15Ni32 forms a disordered ferromagnetic (FM) state that undergoes an FM transition at TC≈ 390 K."

card: Paper card. Question: How can High-Entropy Alloys (HEAs) be designed and optimized to simultaneously achieve high saturation magnetization, high electrical resistivity, and high malleability for soft magnetic material applications?. System: FeCoNi(AlSi)x where x ranges from 0 to 0.8 in molar ratio (alloys denoted A0 to A8). Processing: Arc-melting pure elements (>99.5 wt.% purity) in high-purity argon atmosphere on a water-cooled Cu hearth, remelted four times for homogeneity; rapid solidification into ingots; compressive testing of cylindrical samples (Φ3 × 6 mm) at room temperature with a strain rate of 2 × 10−4 s−1. Test conditions: Room temperature compressive testing; X-ray diffraction (30 kV, 20 mA, Cu target, 10°/min); Electrical resistivity measurement; Magnetization curves via Physical Property Measurement System (PPMS); SEM-EDS microstructural analysis. Findings: The optimal balance of properties is achieved at x = 0.2 (A2 alloy) with saturation magnetization of 1.15 T, coercivity of 1,400 A/m, electrical resistivity of 69.5 μΩ·cm, yield strength of 342 MPa, and strain without fracture of 50%.; Saturation magnetization (Ms) drops almost monotonically from 1.315 T at x = 0 (A0) to 0.46 T at x = 0.8 (A8) upon Al and Si addition.; Alloys with x ≤ 0.2 exhibit a single-phase FCC solid solution, while x = 0.3 shows a BCC + FCC mixture, and x ≥ 0.4 transitions to almost entirely BCC structure.; Plastic deformation (εp) exceeds 50% without fracture for x in the range of 0 to 0.2, whereas ductility diminishes significantly for x ≥ 0.4, with A8 shattering immediately after elastic deformation.; Electrical resistivity generally increases from x = 0 to x = 0.8, reaching 69.5 μΩ·cm at x = 0.2, which falls within the typical range (50–80 μΩ·cm) of silicon steels.; The A3 alloy (x = 0.3) exhibits a yield strength of 938 MPa and ultimate tensile strength of 2,857 MPa with 33% plasticity, attributed to the mixture of FCC and BCC phases.; Coercivity (Hc) is low for x ≤ 0.2 but increases dramatically at x = 0.3 due to phase boundaries hindering domain-wall movement, before falling back at x = 0.5.. Mechanism: High saturation magnetization in FCC structures is attributed to higher atomic packing density (more ferromagnetic atoms per unit volume) and the absence of anti-parallel magnetic coupling elements like Cr; electrical resistivity increases due to lattice distortion from Al/Si, chemical randomness acting as point defects, and electron scattering; mechanical strength and malleability are governed by the phase composition (FCC favors plasticity, BCC increases lattice resistance) and solid-solution strengthening from lattice distortion.. Limitations: The text notes that for x ≥ 0.4, ductility diminishes and samples become brittle; the A8 alloy shatters immediately after elastic deformation; coercivity is highly sensitive to microstructure and difficult to predict solely from composition; ab initio calculations systematically overestimate saturation magnetization compared to experiments due to limited system size and ignored impurities/phase segregation.. Future work: The authors suggest that coercivity can be tuned within a wide range at a given composition by controlling quenching rates and applying heat/pressure treatments to further reduce Hc; the insights on composition-dependent structures and properties can guide the design of structural and functional HEAs and the development of high-entropy soft magnetic materials.. Quote: "the optimal balance of magnetic, electrical, and mechanical properties is achieved at x = 0.2, for which the combination of saturation magnetization (1.15 T), coercivity (1,400 A/m), electrical resistivity (69.5 μΩ·cm), yield strength (342 MPa), and strain without fracture (50%) makes the alloy an excellent SMM."

card: Paper card. Question: How does the substitution of ferromagnetic Co with antiferromagnetic Cr, combined with annealing temperature, influence the hierarchical phase decomposition, microstructure, and resulting magnetic and mechanical properties in AlCoFeNi-based high entropy alloys?. System: AlCoFeNi (x=1) and AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi (x=0.5) high entropy alloys. Processing: Arc melting of elemental pellets (99.9% purity) under argon atmosphere followed by isothermal annealing at 600 °C and 1000 °C for 15 h and water quenching. Test conditions: Annealing at 600 °C/15 h and 1000 °C/15 h; characterization via SEM, EBSD, TEM, APT, Vickers microhardness, and magnetic saturation/coercivity measurements. Findings: AlCoFeNi annealed at 1000 °C forms a single ordered B2 phase with a microhardness of 406 VHN and saturation magnetization of 112 emu/g.; AlCoFeNi annealed at 600 °C decomposes into a B2 + BCC mixture with a microhardness of 474 VHN.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 1000 °C exhibits coarse B2 + BCC phase separation with grain boundary FCC phases.; AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi annealed at 600 °C shows a hierarchical microstructure with decomposition length scales ranging from ~3–5 nm (APT) to ~50–100 nm (TEM) to micron-scale lamellae.; The AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi alloy annealed at 600 °C achieved the highest microhardness of 475 VHN.; Saturation magnetization of the Cr-containing alloy (AlCo0.5Cr0.5FeNi) is reduced by more than 50% compared to the Cr-free alloy due to the antiferromagnetic nature of Cr.; Coercivity decreases with increasing annealing temperature, dropping from 15 Oe at 600 °C to 4 Oe at 1000 °C for the AlCoFeNi alloy.; APT cluster analysis detected Cr-rich BCC precipitates with concentrations ranging from 16% to 74% depending on the generation scale.. Mechanism: The addition of Cr enhances phase separation due to the positive enthalpy of mixing in Fe-Cr, Co-Cr, and Ni-Cr systems, which creates miscibility gaps, whereas the Al-Cr system has a negative enthalpy of mixing favoring compound formation; the length scale of decomposition is controlled by the interplay of composition and annealing temperature.. Limitations: The thermodynamic model predicted an FCC phase in AlCoFeNi at 1000 °C which was not observed experimentally, likely due to a high nucleation barrier; the specific thermodynamic basis for Cr's influence on phase separation in these complex multi-component alloys requires further analysis beyond the scope of the paper.. Future work: Further detailed investigation is required to understand the relationship between B2 phase decomposition into a two-phase B2 + BCC microstructure and the resulting coercivity; the details of the thermodynamic basis underlying the influence of Cr on phase separation require analysis beyond the current scope.. Quote: "The length scale of this decomposition is determined by the combination of composition and annealing temperature."

card: Paper card. Question: How do longitudinal spin fluctuations (LSFs) influence the magnetic structure, phase stability, stacking fault energy, and interfacial energy of the paramagnetic CoCrFeMnNi high entropy alloy across different temperatures and volumes?. System: Equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi (Cantor alloy) in face-centered cubic (fcc) and hexagonal close-packed (hcp) structures. Processing: First-principles alloy theory using density-functional theory (DFT) with the exact muffin-tin orbitals (EMTO) method, generalized gradient approximation (PBE), and the disordered local moment (DLM) picture combined with the coherent-potential approximation (CPA); LSFs modeled via the 'fluctuating medium approximation' and 'one shot from static equilibrium approach' over a temperature range of 50–1200 K and varying Wigner-Seitz radii.. Test conditions: Temperature range 50–1200 K; Wigner-Seitz radii varying to simulate lattice expansion; comparison between fcc and hcp crystal structures; inclusion of experimentally determined thermal lattice expansion.. Findings: LSFs induce sizable magnetic moments for Co, Cr, and Ni in both fcc and hcp phases, whereas these elements show zero or negligible moments in conventional floating spin (FS) calculations.; The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc phase at low temperatures and small volumes, leading to negative stacking fault energy at cryogenic conditions.; The stacking fault energy (γisf) increases monotonically with temperature, rising from −17 mJ m−2 at 50 K to 31 mJ m−2 at 1000 K in the LSF scheme.; The critical temperature for the fcc-hcp phase transition at ambient pressure is predicted to be ~430 K in LSF calculations and ~438 K in FS calculations.; LSFs reduce the magnetic entropy contribution to the stacking fault energy but increase the internal energy contribution, with the positive temperature dependence of γisf dominated by magneto-volume coupling.; The fcc-hcp interfacial energy (σ) slightly decreases with temperature, varying in the range of ~3.1–6.0 mJ m−2 for LSF calculations between 50 and 1200 K.; The difference in mean magnetic moments between fcc and hcp phases is small, amounting to ~0.05–0.23 μB at 100 K and reducing further as temperature increases.. Mechanism: The authors attribute the temperature-dependent behavior to the interplay between magneto-volume coupling and longitudinal spin fluctuations. LSFs induce thermal magnetic moments in elements like Cr and Ni that are otherwise non-magnetic in static calculations, which alters the magnetic entropy and internal energy contributions to the free energy. The hcp phase becomes stable at low temperatures due to these energetic shifts, resulting in negative stacking fault energy that promotes nano-twin and stacking fault formation. As temperature rises, the stacking fault energy becomes positive, suppressing these defects.. Limitations: The explicit phonon effect is not considered in the theory, which may contribute to the discrepancy between the predicted critical temperature (~430 K) and the experimental value (~633 K). The structural relaxation in the faulted supercell was omitted, and an ideal c/a ratio of 8/3 was assumed for the hcp structure.. Future work: The text does not explicitly state future work proposed by the authors beyond the current study's scope.. Quote: "The hcp phase is energetically preferable to the fcc one at cryogenic temperatures, which results in negative stacking fault energy at these conditions."
